title: Michigan avoids disaster via all-time controversial call
summary: Western Michigan got robbed of an all-time upset, with an all-time replay blunder.
full_text: Thirty-two years after Colorado stunned Michigan with a Kordell Stewart to Michael Westbrook Hail Mary at the Big House, Michigan got a Hail Mary win of its own against Western Michigan, a 28.5-point underdog. The victory snatched from the jaws of embarrassment comes with a major asterisk. The final-play touchdown pass from Bryce Underwood to J.J. Buchanahan happened after a highly questionable review restored one second on the clock for a last-gasp effort by the home team, giving Michigan an undeserved mulligan. The entire purpose of replay review is to correct clear and obvious errors made by the officials on the field. In this specific case, there seemed to be no error whatsoever — clear, obvious, or otherwise. The clock struck zero before the ball, which had been thrown out of the end zone, was touched. The game was over. The last gasp was a gift from the football gods for Michigan, and a royal screw job for a Western Michigan team that had earned the win. At a time when there's nearly as much college-football action in court as there is on the field, Western Michigan should be dialing up Judge Wapner in an effort to secure the upset win that a nameless, faceless replay specialist stole from them. While there's surely no procedure in place to correct the outcome, there should be — and maybe the outcry from this outcome will lead to a solution for fixing clear and obvious errors made by the replay process on what should have been the final play of a game. In the age of widespread legalized and normalized gambling, there must be a way to fix such a blatant blunder.
author: Mike Florio

title: Lane Kiffin at halftime of 31-3 blowout: "Imagine if we had pro players"
summary: Some regard LSU coach Lane Kiffin as an agent of chaos.
full_text: Some regard LSU coach Lane Kiffin as an agent of chaos. The better explanation is that he's a garden-variety troll. At halftime of Saturday night's weather-delayed game against Clemson, Kiffin was interviewed by ESPN's Holly Rowe. After the interview ended, Kiffin started to walk away before circling back to the microphone and saying, " Imagine if we had pro players ." It was a hilarious reference to the elephant that has resided in the room for the past several weeks. Kiffin has been trying to add players who should have been eligible for another season, and who pursued NFL careers until their right to one more college season was recognized by the courts. It has sparked outcries from many that "professional" players should be excluded from college football — which ignores the reality that college players are now professional players. Without the two players that LSU decided not to add to the roster for the opening game, given the possibility that the SEC could retaliate by kicking them out of the conference, Kiffin and company are still manhandling Clemson.
author: Mike Florio

title: Harrison Smith returning to Vikings on one-year deal
summary: The veteran safety will be back with Minnesota for his 15th pro season.
full_text: ' As it turns out, Harrison Smith isn't quite done yet. According to a report from NFL Network, Smith is signing a one-year contract to return to the Vikings for 2026. The deal is worth $12.25 million with a maximum value of $16.25 million. Smith, 37, appeared in 15 games with two starts for Minnesota last season, recording 10 passes defensed, two interceptions, a forced fumble, and a sack. The six-time Pro Bowler has spent his entire career with the Vikings, who selected him at No. 29 overall back in 2012. Smith has recorded 39 career interceptions, which ranks No. 4 in franchise history. He’s one away from tying Ed Sharockman for No. 3 on the franchise list, which is led by Paul Krause with 53.
author: Myles Simmons

title: Arch Manning throws for 305 yards and 4 touchdowns against overmatched Texas State
summary: Texas quarterback Arch Manning, the betting favorite to be the first overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft, had an easy start to his season today.
full_text: ' Texas quarterback Arch Manning, the betting favorite to be the first overall pick in the 2027 NFL draft, had an easy start to his season today. Against an overmatched Texas State team, Manning completed 20 of 27 passes for 305 yards, with four touchdowns and one interception, before exiting in the third quarter while Texas led 42-7. Manning and Texas have one of the most talented teams in college football, while Texas State is a mid-level team in the Sun Belt Conference. Manning passed his first test of the season, but it was an easy test. That will change next week, when Manning's Longhorns face No. 1 Ohio State in one of the biggest games of this college football season. Last year, Manning struggled as Texas lost 14-7 at Ohio State. This year, the game is at Texas, Manning is a more experienced and seasoned quarterback, and it's shaping up to potentially be a huge opportunity for Manning to show that he's the best quarterback in college football.
author: Michael David Smith

title: Patriots RB TreVeyon Henderson still not practicing with ankle injury
summary: Henderson hurt his ankle during practice on August 24 and hasn't practiced since.
full_text: Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson is still not practicing as he deals with an ankle injury. Henderson was not participating in the Patriots' practice today, according to reporters on the scene. Henderson hurt his ankle during practice on August 24 and hasn't practiced since. It remains unclear whether Henderson will be able to go for Wednesday's regular-season opener against the Seahawks. The Patriots' first official practice report of the season has not yet been released. Henderson led the Patriots with 180 carries for 911 yards and nine touchdowns last season. If he can't go, Rhamondre Stevenson would be the primary ball carrier against the Seahawks, and Corey Kiner, who arrived in a trade with the Cardinals next week, would be No. 2. The Patriots would likely call up either Hassan Haskins or Lan Larison from the practice squad if Henderson isn't active against the Seahawks.
author: Michael David Smith

title: USC draws a bigger crowd (but not by much) to second home game
summary: Last Saturday, USC had a poor turnout for its home opener at the L.A.
full_text: Last Saturday, USC had a poor turnout for its home opener at the L.A. Coliseum — so poor that the school issued a statement about it. On Friday, the Trojans had a better showing. But not by much. Via the New York Post , USC announced a crowd of 53,014 for the Fresno State game. The San Jose State game had an official attendance of 51,114. The stadium holds 71,349 for USC games. The actual tickets scanned for the San Jose State game, per the Post, were only 35,585. For the Fresno State game, that number increased to 45,833. Coach Lincoln Riley has pushed back on the narrative that interest in the program is falling. “I think that comes from a lot of people who don’t follow our program, most of those who have never stepped foot in the Coliseum,” Riley recently said. “The reality is, during my years here, attendance has gone up every single year. As has our play in the Coliseum, including running the table last year in front of a lot of epic atmospheres. And I expect that to happen again this year.” The next opportunity arrives in seven days, against Louisiana. Two weeks later, No. 2 Oregon visits — followed by No. 17 Washington. Games against No. 1 Ohio State and Maryland round out the seven-game home slate.
author: Mike Florio

title: 49ers place DE Sam Okuayinonu on IR
summary: 49ers defensive end Sam Okuayinonu won't play against the Rams on Thursday and he will miss at least three more games as well.
full_text: '' 49ers defensive end Sam Okuayinonu won't play against the Rams on Thursday and he will miss at least three more games as well. The 49ers announced that they placed Okuayinonu on injured reserve on Saturday. They also announced the previously reported signing of defensive end Khalid Kareem off of the Falcons' practice squad. Okuayinonu is out with a foot injury. He had 74 tackles, six sacks and two forced fumbles in 31 games for the team over the last two seasons. He also had six tackles in two playoff appearances last year. Kareem joins Nick Bosa, Keion White, and Romello Height at defensive end for the 49ers. Bosa is returning from a torn ACL and there's been no definitive word from the team on his status for the opener.
author: Josh Alper

title: Christian Gonzalez doesn't commit to playing season opener
summary: Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez still doesn't have a contract extension, and with the season opener only four days away, he isn't not committing to playing without one.
full_text: ' Patriots cornerback Christian Gonzalez still doesn't have a contract extension, and with the season opener only four days away, he isn't not committing to playing without one. Gonzalez continues to take a day-to-day approach. “ I’m focused on today ,” Gonzalez said, via Doug Kyed of the Boston Herald . “Right now, it is practice in what, a couple, 30 minutes, 40 minutes. Worried on that right now, so we’ll focus on that.” Gonzalez answered "I don't know" when asked if contract talks were progressing. The Seahawks recently signed cornerback Devon Witherspoon to a four-year, $132 million deal, which should provide a template for the Patriots. Gonzalez and Witherspoon have the same agent, Reggie Johnson. Gonzalez is under contract for the next two seasons and is scheduled to make a base salary of $2.259 million this season. The 17th overall pick in 2023, he made second-team All-Pro in 2024 and the Pro Bowl in 2025. He has totaled 145 tackles, two interceptions, 24 pass breakups and a sack in three seasons. He said Thursday he is "still frustrated" a deal isn't done.
author: Charean Williams

title: Malik Nabers says Odell Beckham was the person who made him start watching football
summary: Nabers says it's "surreal" and "amazing" to have Beckham for a teammate.
full_text: Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers was an 8-year-old in Louisiana when Odell Beckham started playing wide receiver for LSU. Nabers was 11 when Beckham won the NFL's Offensive Rookie of the Year award playing for the Giants. Nabers could only dream that he and Beckham would end up as teammates. Nabers credits Beckham for turning him into a football fan and making him want to be a wide receiver, and Nabers finds it amazing that he ended up playing for LSU, then the Giants, and now being Beckham's teammate in 2026. "He kind of was the base person that literally made me start watching football ," Nabers said, via Jordan Raanan of ESPN. "The dances, the one-handers. And he was probably the first person I started really watching when I started playing football. He was the main person. So, just for him being here right now, in the same room as me, it's surreal. Sometimes I got to take a moment, but to have him here is actually amazing." Nabers is the Giants' No. 1 receiver while Beckham is a backup, but Nabers still looks up to Beckham, as the player who blazed the career trail that Nabers followed.
author: Michael David Smith

title: Lane Kiffin: Leaving former NFL players off roster in best interest of LSU
summary: Kiffin cited "the uncertainties of what could come" as the reason for the decision.
full_text: LSU opted against putting former NFL players Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris on their roster for Saturday's game against Clemson on Friday night and that decision pushed pause on the collision between the school and the Southeastern Conference about their desire to have the players on the field this season. The SEC is opposed to member schools having players who have spent time in the NFL on the roster, but a preliminary injunction in Louisiana barred the conference or the NCAA for penalizing any school that put them on the field. The conference has filed a federal lawsuit to prevent those players from playing and LSU's head coach Lane Kiffin cited "the uncertainties of what could come" as the reason for the decision to keep Wright and Harris off the field during an appearance on ESPN on Saturday morning. Kiffin said that he believes that decision was in the "best interest" of the school, but the players could still be added to the roster at a later date so there's no sign that this is the end of the road. Matt Hayes of USA Today quoted a source saying that they were "not sure LSU would still be a member " of the SEC if the rest of the conference's schools had voted on Friday and ESPN analyst Paul Finebaum suggested the same on air on Saturday. Attorney Ryan Downton, who represents Wright and Harris, said in a statement, via Pete Thamel of ESPN, that LSU made a " measured decision " and that "everyone should use that space to lower the temperature and look at the facts" around the case. Downton went on to make the case by noting neither player made a roster or played in a preseason game and closed the statement by hoping that "level heads prevail." Little about the process thus far suggests that will be the case and the ongoing court cases mean that there's likely a lot more to come in the fight that has taken center stage in college football as the 2026 season gets underway.
author: Josh Alper

title: West Virginia retires Pat White's No. 5 on Saturday
summary: The West Virginia football program hasn't retired many numbers.
full_text: The West Virginia football program hasn't retired many numbers. Only two quarterbacks have gotten the honor. In 2021, WVU retired No. 9 for the 30-years-ahead-of-his-time phenomenon known as Major Harris. Second, as of today, the Mountaineers will retire No. 5 for the incomparable Pat White. White won four bowl games in four years with the Mountaineers, including a win over Georgia in the Sugar Bowl (played that year in Atlanta) and a victory over Oklahoma in the Fiesta Bowl. He also authored a win over Georgia Tech (and Calvin Johnson) in the Gator Bowl, despite trailing 35-17 in the fourth quarter. Here's just a small taste of what he could do. (One of my favorite Pat White highlights didn’t happen on the field .) White finished his four-year career with a record of 35-8. He threw for 6,049 yards and ran for 4,480 — a career average of 6.5 yards per carry. He generated 103 total touchdowns running and passing. NBC's Devin McCourty, who faced White three times while playing for Rutgers, called him "unstoppable." "He was the guy that you thought you had a good game plan for," McCourty said. "On paper, everything was covered and you knew how they were going to attack you. Then the moment came to make the play on him, and it never happened. He made you miss or he made the great throw against good coverage. He was unstoppable." White entered the NFL at a time when the wildcat quarterback was becoming very popular. Drafted 44th overall by the Dolphins in 2009, he made cameo appearances in 13 games as a rookie. A January 2010 concussion that left him unconscious would be his final regular-season appearance. White later played in the UFL, had a short stint with Washington, and finished his career in the CFL. Regardless, White became one of the all-time greatest college football players, at any school. And if he were playing today, he likely would be scooped up by one of the big-money programs after only one year in Morgantown. That's really the saddest part of the story. White played at a time when college football players weren't getting paid. He never got anything close to the value he generated for West Virginia or for college football generally. Retiring his number is an appropriate gesture, even if the total debt owed by the entire state to White is far greater than that.
author: Mike Florio

title: NFL fines Browns' Tytus Howard $12,537 for tripping
summary: When the NFL fines players during the preseason, when they aren't receiving their regular paychecks, the fines are typically for lower amounts.
full_text: When the NFL fines players during the preseason, when they aren't receiving their regular paychecks, the fines are typically for lower amounts. But Browns offensive lineman Tytus Howard got a fairly substantial preseason fine. The NFL fined Howard $12,537 for what it deemed unnecessary roughness during the first quarter of the first preseason game. Howard got a 15-yard penalty for tripping on the play. The $12,537 fine was the biggest fine the NFL has announced for the 2026 preseason, although the league has not yet announced any fines for the third and final week of the preseason. The league's ability to fine players is established in the Collective Bargaining Agreement with the players' union. The NFL's officiating department reviews plays and refers potential fines to the football operations staff, which then examines the plays in question to determine whether a fine is in order. Players who get fined are sent a letter informing them of the fine and a video of the play in question. Players who don't appeal have the money withheld from their next game check. Players who do appeal fines get a hearing with an appeals officer who is jointly appointed by the NFL and the NFL Players Association. This season, the appeals officers are Derrick Brooks, Jordy Nelson and James Thrash. The appeals officer has final say. Fine money is donated to the Professional Athletes Foundation, which supports former players in need, and the NFL Foundation, which supports health and safety initiatives in football from youth leagues to the professional level.
author: Michael David Smith

title: Deion Sanders didn't have to testify in the Shilo Sanders bankruptcy trial
summary: Thursday was a good day for Deion Sanders, on two counts.
full_text: Thursday was a good day for Deion Sanders, on two counts. First, his Colorado team upset Georgia Tech to start the season 1-0. Second, the judge presiding over Shilo Sanders's bankruptcy trial decided that Deion wouldn't be required to testify in the case. Via Brent Schrotenboer of USA Today , the presiding judge declared on Thursday that Deion was released from his subpoena . The day didn't go as well in court for Shilo. As Schrotenboer explains, a witness called by Shilo's lawyers offered contradictory testimony on a key question in the case of whether injuries inflicted by Shilo on John Darjean, a security guard at his school, were "willful and malicious." The witness, Ruda Nash James, testified that she saw Darjean choking Shilo. During the testimony, Darjean's lawyer played a recording of a phone call between James and Shilo's mother from the day of the 2015 incident. "Did you see his hand around Shilo’s neck?” Pilar Sanders asked James. “I didn’t see the neck part,” James said. “I didn’t see all that.” Oops. Separately, Shilo's lawyer was stopped by the judge (who will be deciding the case) from questioning Darjean about the possibility that his injuries were the result of his baseball career. As the judge pointed out, the current case isn't about whether the fight with Shilo caused injuries that culminated in an $11.89 million judgment that created the debt Shilo hopes to discharge through bankruptcy. It's only about whether the injuries were willfully or maliciously inflicted. The biggest bit of drama on Thursday happened when Darjean collapsed after testifying, apparently due to his chronic pain. It appears that the case was paused on Friday. Eventually, the judge will decide whether Shilo will, or won't, carry the $11.89 million debt moving forward.
author: Mike Florio

title: Miami Hurricanes linebacker Mohamed Toure starts his eighth year of college football
summary: As controversy about player eligibility embroils college football, LSU has decided not to play two former NFL players today.
full_text: As controversy about player eligibility embroils college football, LSU has decided not to play two former NFL players today. But another player whose eligibility demonstrates major changes in the NCAA was on the field for the Miami Hurricanes' opener on Friday night. Miami linebacker Mohamed Toure recorded five tackles in Friday night's win over Stanford, which is noteworthy because this is Toure's eighth season playing college football. Before transferring to Miami last year, Toure had been on the team at Rutgers for six years. Toure announced in January that he would return to the Hurricanes for the 2026 season, and unlike the issue of former NFL players, there wasn't even any controversy about it because the NCAA made clear that he's eligible for an eighth season — something that once would have been unthinkable in college football. Here's how every year of Toure's college football career has unfolded: In 2019, Toure enrolled at Rutgers and played two games as a freshman. At the time, the rules said that he could take that year as a redshirt and play four more years after that, so his eligibility would be used up after the 2023 season. In 2020, Toure played nine games for Rutgers, but the NCAA decided not to count that season toward any player’s eligibility because of the impact that covid had on the 2020 season. In 2021, Toure played 13 games for Rutgers. As far as the NCAA was concerned, this was the first year that counted toward his four years of eligibility. In 2022, Toure missed the season with an injury. In the old days, the redshirt year he took in 2019 would have meant he couldn’t take another medical redshirt, but under the newer rules, the NCAA didn’t count 2022 toward his eligibility limit. So through four years at Rutgers, he had still used only one year of NCAA eligibility. In 2023, Toure played 13 games for Rutgers. This previously would have been his final year of eligibility, but the NCAA now calls that only the second year that counted toward his eligibility. In 2024, Toure again missed the season with an injury. The NCAA once again allowed that to be yet another medical redshirt year that didn’t count toward his eligibility, so after his sixth year in college football he had still only used two years of eligibility. In 2025, Toure transferred after six years at Rutgers to Miami, where he was a team captain who helped the Hurricanes get to the College Football National Championship Game. That was his seventh year in college football and his third year of eligibility. And now in 2026, Toure is one of the Hurricanes' top players, in his eighth year of college football and his fourth and — we think — final year of NCAA eligibility.
author: Michael David Smith

title: Vikings legend Harrison Smith returning to Minnesota on a one-year deal, per report
summary: The 37-year-old safety, who leads all active players with 39 career interceptions, returns for his 15th season on a $12.25 million deal to anchor Minnesota's defense.
full_text:
The Minnesota Vikings are bringing back former All-Pro safety Harrison Smith on a one-year, $12.25 million deal, according to NFL Media .
A bonafide Vikings legend, the 37-year-old Smith will return to Minnesota for his 15th NFL season. During his first 14 seasons with the Vikings, Smith -- the 12th overall pick in the 2012 NFL Draft out of Notre Dame -- was a six-time Pro Bowler and one-time All-Pro. Each of Smith's Pro Bowl nods took place from 2015-21. He was a first-team All-Pro in 2017 while helping the Vikings advance to within a game of the Super Bowl .
Smith is renowned for his impressive production across the board. His 39 career interceptions are the most in the NFL among active players. He also has 1,180 career tackles (51 for loss), 21.5 sacks, 13 forced fumbles, 10 fumble recoveries, 106 pass breakups and four interception returns for scores.
While he hasn't been named to a Pro Bowl since 2021, Smith has continued to be a productive player. In 15 games last season, Smith filled the stat sheet with two interceptions, 10 pass breakups, a forced fumble, a fumble recovery and 54 tackles.
Smith will re-join a Vikings defense that invested heavily on the defensive side of the ball during April's draft. Minnesota drafted five defensive players that included first-round pick Caleb Banks and fellow defensive backs Jakobe Thomas and Charles Demmings .
Minnesota opens the 2026 season home against the Packers on Sept. 13.
author: Bryan DeArdo

title: Browns offensive lineman receives NFL's first big fine of 2026 season
summary: Players usually aren't fined this much during the preseason
full_text:
Tytus Howard is the unenviable recipient of the NFL's biggest fine of the 2026 season thus far. The Cleveland Browns ' veteran offensive lineman received a rather hefty fine by the league stemming from his actions during Cleveland's preseason opener against the Chicago Bears on Aug. 15.
The NFL fined Howard $12,537 for what it deemed unnecessary roughness during the first quarter of Cleveland's eventual 34-10 loss in the Windy City. Howard was penalized 15 yards for tripping during the first play of the Browns' second possession. Despite the penalty, the Browns scored their first points of the preseason when kicker Andre Szmyt ended the drive with a 50-yard field goal.
Howard's fine is larger than typical preseason fines. Of the 25 players who have been fined this , only two players have received fines that exceeded $10,000. The only other player who has exceeded that total is Tennessee Titans outside linebacker Oluwafemi Oladejo, who was docked $10,625 for a face mask penalty.
The 25 players were fined a total of $163,513, which averages out to $6,541 per player. According to Pro Football Talk , the league's fine money is donated to the Professional Athletes Foundation, which supports former players in need, and the NFL Foundation, which supports health and safety initiatives in football from youth leagues to the professional level.
Howard, 30, signed a two-year, $45 million contract shortly after he was traded from Houston to Cleveland back in March. The 23rd overall pick in the 2019 NFL Draft, Howard has started in each of his 97 regular-season games (including the postseason). He started in 20 games each of the last two seasons that included four playoff games.

title: Agent's Take: How the Rams built a salary-cap super team around Matthew Stafford
summary: Here's how the Rams fit their stars under the salary cap and what the spending spree means for their future
full_text:
A 31-27 loss to the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC Championship Game was considered by the Los Angeles Rams as a missed opportunity because their NFC West divisional rival dominated the New England Patriots to win Super Bowl LX. Once 2025 NFL MVP Matthew Stafford quickly decided to return for an 18th season, the Rams swung for the fences to capitalize.
The only unrestricted free agent of consequence was safety Kam Curl. He was retained on a three-year, $36 million contract, with up to $39 million in salary escalators.
Cornerback, the most glaring roster weakness, was upgraded in a trade and through free agency. Trent McDuffie , who was entering a contract year, was acquired from the Kansas City Chiefs in March. He signed a four-year, $124 million contract extension in connection with the trade, making him the NFL's highest-paid cornerback at the time. Jaylen Watson , McDuffie's cornerback counterpart in Kansas City, received a three-year, $51 million deal as an unrestricted free agent.
Another order of business was adjusting Stafford's contract. As the 2025 NFL MVP, Stafford was still underpaid despite renegotiating the final two years of the four-year, $160 million extension he signed in 2022, which had $58 million remaining, into a two-year, $84 million deal last year. Stafford received a one-year extension for $55 million running through the 2027 season. Incentives make Stafford's extension worth up to $60 million.
A persistent pursuit of edge rusher Myles Garrett , which began in 2022, finally paid dividends in June. The Cleveland Browns dealt the reigning NFL Defensive Player of the Year to the Rams for a 2027 first-round pick, a 2028 second-round pick, a 2029 third-round pick and edge rusher Jared Verse , who was 2024's NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year.
The Garrett acquisition had an unexpected major consequence. His addition inspired defensive tackle Aaron Donald , who was on track to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer in 2029, to unretire.
After winning the offseason, the Rams are heavy favorites to be Super Bowl LXI champions at 5-to-1, according to SportsLine. The Buffalo Bills have the next best odds at 10-to-1, followed by the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks.
The Rams assembled a team more reminiscent of a previous era before the salary cap was implemented in 1994. The NFL salary cap is $301.2 million for the 2026 league year. Each team's actual salary cap (known as adjusted salary cap) is typically different from the NFL's set amount because unused cap room can be carried over from one year to the next year and other adjustments can further increase or decrease cap space.
The Rams have an adjusted salary cap of $313.324 million. The league-wide average is $317.822 million according to NFLPA data. The New England Patriots have the NFL's highest adjusted salary cap at $352.979 million, largely thanks to carrying over $47.27 million of cap room, which is easily the most in the league. The Bills have the lowest at $301.58 million, which is only $380,000 above the league-wide number.
The Rams constructed a roster that is top-heavy, salary-cap-wise. Stafford has the 2026 largest cap number at $48,267,348. The only other 2026 cap number above $45 million belongs to Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert with $46.35 million.
Wide receiver Davante Adams and left tackle Alaric Jackson's Jackson have the 25th- and 35th-highest cap numbers in the NFL for 2026. Adams has the third-highest wide receiver figure at $28 million. Jackson's $25.4 million is fifth among offensive linemen (fourth for an offensive tackle).
Four other Rams have 2026 cap numbers that rank among the 10 highest at their respective positions. Kyren Williams , who signed a three-year, $33 million extension last July, has the third-biggest running back cap number at $11.7 million. Coleman Shelton's $9.5 million is fourth for a center. Kevin Dotson's $17.4 million is the seventh-largest offensive guard cap hit. Colby Parkinson has the ninth-highest tight end cap figure ($9.1 million).
The collective $48 million average yearly salary of McDuffie and Watson for the upgrade at cornerback is the NFL's second-highest, behind only the Indianapolis Colts tandem of Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward at $48.1 million. McDuffie's and Watson's combined $17.8 million 2026 cap hit is smaller than Ward's alone ($19.9 million). Their cap figures will jump significantly in 2027. McDuffie's will be a cornerback, high $30.8 million, while Watson's $22.7 million ranks 10th.
Garrett had five years worth $179 million remaining on his contract when acquired. His contract was almost immediately reworked. Instead of making $31.5 million in 2026, his salary was raised to $37 million, with $35.7 million converted into a signing bonus that would be prorated at $7.14 million annually against the salary cap from 2026 through 2030. His 2026 cap number is $8,840,680.
Garrett's 2027 compensation drops from $42.7 million to $32 million, while his 2028 money increases to $30 million from $24.8 million. His compensation for 2029 and 2030 remains at $40 million in each year.
There are two separate option bonuses, each for $15 million in 2027, to pick up dummy/voiding 2031 and 2032 contract years. Because this $30.145 million is being prorated on the salary cap from 2027 through 2031 at $6.029 million annually, Garrett's 2027 cap hit is $15.024 million. Given the market for elite pass rushers has changed dramatically since Garrett became the NFL's first $40 million per year non-quarterback in March 2025, it wouldn't be surprising for his deal to be renegotiated as early as next year.
The Rams had more than $15 million in existing cap space, according to NFLPA data, when Donald decided to come out of retirement on August 30. The Rams had retained his contractual rights when he retired after the 2023 season by placing him on the reserve/retired list. The remaining year left on his contract tolled or was frozen.
Because of some creative salary cap maneuvering when Donald retired in 2024, the Rams easily handled his contract upon reinstatement without anymore salary cap gymnastics. Donald's 2026 salary was just his league minimum $1.3 million before he and the Rams agreed on a one-year, $20 million deal worth a maximum of $30 million through incentives.
The $20 million is composed of a fully guaranteed $10 million base salary and $10 million in per-game roster bonuses, with $666,666.67 for each game on the 53-man roster, capped at 15 games. The $10 million in incentives is primarily tied to Donald's playtime and the Rams' postseason success. Donald gets $2.5 million if he has at least 15% of the defensive snaps in the regular season and the Rams make the playoffs. There's $1.25 million on the Rams' active roster for the wild card game or if a bye is earned for that playoff round. Being on the active roster for a divisional playoff game is worth another $1.25 million. Donald gets $2.5 million each for an NFC Championship Game win and a Super Bowl win, provided his regular-season defensive playtime reached 15% and he took at least 20% of the defensive snaps in the requisite game.
Technically, Donald is under contract for 2027 at his $1.345 million league minimum salary, and there are dummy/voiding 2028 through 2030 contract years. Donald has a $5.826 million 2026 cap number because his low 2027 salary triggered an obscure salary cap rule, the 50% Down Rule. Since Donald's second-year salary in 2027 is less than half of his first-year salary in 2026, the difference between the two salaries, including the $3.75 million of Donald's incentives classified as likely to be earned, is being treated as a signing bonus and prorated over these five years. As a result, Donald's 2026 cap number consists of $1.3 million categorized as base salary and $4.481 million as bonus proration. The $4.481 million of bonus proration applies to 2027 as well as each of the dummy/voiding 2028 through 2030 contract years.

title: Cardinals’ Jacoby Brissett has an ace in the hole
summary: Now that the final roster has taken shape for the Arizona Cardinals, leading up to the Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers, the new offense is either taking shape or it isn’t. Most of the offense has been together for training camp, several preseason games, OTAs and minicamps. Except for quarterback Jacoby Brissett. […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Jacoby Brissett #7 of the Arizona Cardinals reacts after his team's touchdown against the Las Vegas Raiders in the second quarter of the preseason game at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images Now that the final roster has taken shape for the Arizona Cardinals, leading up to the Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers, the new offense is either taking shape or it isn’t. Most of the offense has been together for training camp, several preseason games, OTAs and minicamps. Except for quarterback Jacoby Brissett. RELATED: CARDINALS EXTEND MICHAEL WILSON Brissett is the undisputed starting quarterback. This is in spite of the fact that both Gardner Minshew and rookie Carson Beck have gotten all of the tutelage of the new offense in all of the offseason activities. New head coach Mike LaFleur was brought in to jump-start the offensive side of the ball. This came with a plan. Because LaFleur came from the coaching tree of both Sean McVay and Kyle Shanahan, it was his duty to install a new offense. Freshly shorn QB Jacoby Brissett ready for the #AZCardinals season. pic.twitter.com/ExXd1By2Ks — Darren Urban (@Cardschatter) September 1, 2026 But installing a new offense is intricate and complex. It isn’t something that Cliff Notes will completely educate each of the players whose job it is to learn it. Meetings are helpful, and, of course, playbook study. Then the main tutelage has to come during practice sessions. You can’t cook a meal without turning on the stove first. Which circles back to Brissett. As quarterback, he must command the huddle and become the undisputed leader. That also comes with the responsibility of knowing what the hell he is doing. He can’t call plays and then question what comes next, or what everybody on the field, for that matter, should be doing. Other players only need to know what they are doing on each play and where they should end up. But not the quarterback. He has to know everyone’s responsibility on each play called. But didn’t Brissett miss all of the offseason in an effort to bolster his bank account? And while that was a success, what about the reason he is here in the first place? Getting down this new offense, remember? When Brissett finally came back to the team, he was pretty far behind the learning curve. Just exactly how is he supposed to cram for the exam? Wearing those multi-page wrist cuffs? Well, Brissett has a tool. Well, call it more of an asset. He has aligned himself with QB coach Matt Schaub. Ever since Brissett inked his new deal, he has been working overtime to get to know all of the nuances of this new offense. Both LaFleur and Schaub didn’t start with the basics with Brissett, mainly because he is an 11-year veteran who has played in multiple systems and is known as a quick-learning student. This is fortunate for both the player and the coaching staff. Schaub has been Brissett’s shadow since he showed up. The first step was to learn the new verbiage instead of calling plays by what things were called last season. This process didn’t happen overnight, but along with the new offense, it has its own terminology that must be adhered to by all so that everyone is on the same page. A new same page, that is. Since Schaub has been in similar situations during his 16-year career, having played under five systems himself and having to adjust to many different offensive coordinators, he has become an excellent tutor for Brissett. Both are smart guys. And since Schaub is a former quarterback, he has real-life experiences that he is able to pass along. The two are also able to discuss schemes that only quarterbacks can understand and absorb. With Schaub’s help, Brissett is getting the terminology down and is learning the offense. Getting comfortable with everyone’s role is still a difficult ask. With Schaub’s continued assistance, running and operating as a very good offense is the ultimate goal. The coaches haven’t held back with Brissett, and he has responded. He has been in extra meetings, extra walk-throughs, and endless discussions and countless questions. The chats are different than the ones Schaub has with the other two quarterbacks, especially the rookie Beck. The discussions aren’t as detailed or bogged down with wordy structures that may muddle the young talent. This Cardinals team may or may not flourish this season. It will come down to the offensive line, which has added three new members to the starting rotation. But let it be known, this offense is absolutely stacked with talent. For Brissett, repetitions on the field have been the key to learning this new offense. He has been going through the play calls in his head, having physical walk-throughs, and finally actual practice reps. From his footwork to progressions, Schaub is right there to offer a suggestion or to simply tell him about issues that he is seeing that need a tweak or an alteration. The two signalcallers are working longer hours than anyone else, and hopefully it will pay off. Will Brissett have everything down when Week 1 rolls around? Probably not. But he won’t be viewed as a work in progress either. He will be more of a man and his shadow.

title: The Falcoholic Reacts: An explosive defensive tackle combo
summary: Several new players make up the Falcons’ interior tackle rotation this season. After struggling to stop the run last season, the team is optimistic that a personnel overhaul will help address a major flaw. They have gotten younger by trading for Gervon Dexter Sr. and Maason Smith. These look like well-calculated moves by Ian Cunningham […]
full_text: Several new players make up the Falcons’ interior tackle rotation this season. After struggling to stop the run last season, the team is optimistic that a personnel overhaul will help address a major flaw. They have gotten younger by trading for Gervon Dexter Sr. and Maason Smith. These look like well-calculated moves by Ian Cunningham to bolster a group that needs to carry the load early in the season. They will join Brandon Dorlus, who finished second on the team in sacks with 8.5. Dorlus may occasionally shift to the edge, but the coaching staff knows how prolific he can be as an interior pass rusher. That is why fans firmly believe he will play the most snaps out of all the defensive tackles. The question is who plays more between Dexter Sr. and Smith. The answer proved to be more definitive than expected. Despite falling out of favor in Chicago, Dexter Sr. is expected to take on a major role after recently joining the Falcons. His intriguing pass-rushing skills feature a quick first step and impressive bend to beat opposing guards. Combining his attributes with Dorlus could provide Jeff Ulbrich’s defense with the punch inside that compensates for the lack of viable edge-rushing options. This result is brought to you by FanDuel Sportsbook.

title: Falcons don’t have a QB controversy; they have a leadership vacuum
summary: The Atlanta Falcons are the only NFL team still trying to figure out who their starting quarterback will be for Week 1. It’s unprecedented to be this late in the process and still not have figured out whether Michael Penix or Tua Tagovailoa will be their guy. Cameron Wolfe of NFL Network recently reported that […]
full_text: The Atlanta Falcons are the only NFL team still trying to figure out who their starting quarterback will be for Week 1. It’s unprecedented to be this late in the process and still not have figured out whether Michael Penix or Tua Tagovailoa will be their guy. Cameron Wolfe of NFL Network recently reported that the team eventually wants Penix to be the starter, but without a clean bill of health, they aren’t willing to move forward with that yet. Penix was recently cleared for 11-on-11 practices and, in the days since, has split first-team reps with Tua. The team could make this a lot easier, but with most things involving the Atlanta Falcons, whether it be winning games or recovering onside kicks , they have to make it more difficult than it needs to be. The simple solution should be to say Penix is the starter, but until he’s comfortable and ready to play, Tua, as the backup, will play. But it’s likely the thing stopping the team from adopting this simple solution is that they’re not yet convinced Penix should be their guy. Why? This delay clearly shows a lack of a cohesive, coordinated vision by head coach Kevin Stefanski, GM Ian Cunningham, and former Falcons QB1 Matt Ryan, the newly dubbed President of Football for the entire universe. Why a delayed QB1 decision signals leadership’s disconnect Penix is clearly the correct answer to be the team’s starter for the bulk of 2026, because he raises the ceiling for the Falcons offense. We know Stefanski values accuracy above all else in his quarterbacks , and that’s an area where Penix is lacking compared to Tua. However, ball placement is one of the only areas of quarterback play where Tua outshines Penix. In any other objective measure, Penix is the better option for the Falcons. So if Stefanski can’t put his preferences aside for the greater good of the team, it raises major red flags over whether he’s the right man to lead Atlanta out of their eight-year playoff drought. Penix’s superior arm strength and willingness to attack downfield are critical areas that make him a better quarterback option. There has been an evolution in NFL defenses over the past decade, with a shift toward two-high shells due to concerns about giving up explosive plays. Without the vertical element in your passing game, you’re making it too easy for NFL defenses. Tua’s efficient dink-and-dunk style can lead to chunk yards if he’s throwing the ball underneath to explosive playmakers like Bijan Robinson and Zachariah Branch, given their dynamic run-after-catch abilities. But that’s a hard way to live in the modern NFL, especially when there have been copious amounts of data-driven analysis that says explosive plays are critical to putting points on the scoreboard. Penix’s arm strength and willingness to push the ball vertically clearly give the Falcons offense a much higher ceiling. The math favors Penix’s avoidance of drive killers Penix is also less prone than Tua to the negative plays that kill drives , such as sacks and turnovers. Tua takes a much higher number of sacks whenever pressured, recording a 19.4 percent career pressure-to-sack rate according to PFF , compared to Penix’s 12.2 percent. Tagovailoa is coming off a career-worst 23 percent in 2025, culminating a three-year downward trend in that metric. Penix has ranked in the top 7 among all quarterbacks with the lowest pressure-to-sack rate in each of his first two seasons. Which isn’t some two-year quirk or anomaly given that he led the nation in that metric in 2022 at Washington, and was top 10 in his final year in 2023. Even with the limited mobility, Penix knows how to avoid sacks. Tua has a 4 percent turnover-worthy play rate over his career per PFF compared to Penix’s 2.9 percent. For comparison’s sake, Kirk Cousins finished with a rate of 4.6 in 2024. Essentially, those numbers tell you that a “normal” season for Tua closely resembles Kirk’s turnover-laden first year in Atlanta. A one percent difference may seem negligible, but it amounts to six fewer turnover-worthy plays over the course of a season. Given the razor-thin margins that decide NFL outcomes , that is a notable difference. Not to mention, Stefanski led a Cleveland Browns team that routinely shot itself in the foot, ranking fourth-most penalized team over the last six seasons. He should especially be hyper-aware of how detrimental negative plays are to offensive success, given the Browns were also behind the Las Vegas Raiders in the most drives ending in turnovers . Penix’s rookie deal helps Atlanta avoid making Miami’s $200 million mistake And we haven’t even gotten into the fact that Penix is younger and still playing on his rookie contract. This gives the Falcons much greater future flexibility to build out the rest of the roster if he’s successful this season. If Tua is the starter and plays well in 2026, then the Falcons will be forced to give him a lucrative contract extension as he hits free agency next spring. The Falcons have plenty of cap space headed into 2027 , but they should be hesitant to pay Tua. After all, when the Miami Dolphins paid him back in the summer of 2024 , it led to the GM and head coach getting fired within 18 months. Atlanta’s decision-makers should be extremely hesitant to repeat that mistake. The Falcons have a significant financial decision ahead regarding Penix next offseason, too: whether to pick up his fifth-year option for 2028. But they can only make an informed decision if Penix gets plenty of runway to play this season. There’s really no justification for the Falcons to pick Tua over Penix. A simple cost/benefit analysis clearly points in the direction of Penix. The only rationale is if they think Tua is significantly better than Penix. But Tua’s inconsistency throughout the summer highlights why such a belief holds no water. If Tua were a significantly better option than Penix, they would definitively know that by now. Stop overthinking it; ut’s time to be leaders The path forward for the Falcons at quarterback isn’t complicated. Name Penix the starter and say that Tua will play until he’s ready. Since Penix is in no rush to get back on the field before he feels 100 percent coming back from his third ACL tear, you can comfortably give Tua the first-team reps next week in a situation that is no different than if the backup was practicing with the starter injured. The only dilemma would arrive next Wednesday if Penix says he’s not ready yet. And whenever Penix is ready, whether that be Week 1 or later, the Falcons need to make the pivot to see if he’s the long-term successor to Ryan’s mantle as franchise quarterback. If, by season’s end, he’s not the answer, the team can move on, and no one will second-guess the decision. The Falcons’ leadership can firmly say they did what they believed was in the team’s best interest. The decisions will only become much more complex and difficult in the future. Their “quarterback dilemma” is entry-level stuff, and their failure so far to navigate it in a clear and decisive way raises serious doubts about whether the right people are steering this ship. It’s time for the leaders in Flowery Branch to do what they’re paid to do: lead.

full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - JANUARY 17: Tre'Davious White #27 of the Buffalo Bills looks on from the field during an NFL divisional playoff football game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on January 17, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images With Labor Day approaching, there are 3,352 individual snaps from players on last season’s Buffalo Bills defense who are currently unsigned. Those snaps came from eight players; Tre White, Joey Bosa, Matt Milano, Jordan Poyer, DaQuan Jones, Taylor Rapp, Jordan Phillips, and Larry Ogunjobi, I don’t know how often this happens in the NFL, but I assume this type of occurrence is more normal than it originally seems. Having written that, I would bet eight players who played more than 200 snaps (out of 20) on a team that eventually advanced to the divisional round of the playoffs not being on an NFL roster by September 1 the following year is darn rare. This has been something Bills fans — and media — have been tracking for a while this offseason, and justifiably so. Everyone has their own take on what it means, and I don’t necessarily think there’s a correct answer either. Does it clearly show the Bills defensive roster wasn’t good enough last season? Does it demonstrate Sean McDermott got a lot out of the personnel he had? Or, the least discussed, least controversial, and simplest conclusion — does it mean the Bills 2025 defense featured a rather large collection of rosterable players who just so happened to be in the final year of the league deeming they were rosterable? I tend to lean with the latter, and while I can get slightly on board with the idea that McDermott and Co. got the best out of those veterans, we can’t forget the defense was 13th in EPA allowed per play, which included being 7th in EPA per drop back and 31st in EPA per rush (non-garbage time). Plus, it did allow 33 points in the divisional-round loss. But I’m not here to harp on that playoff game now. I want to ask you — what do you think those 2025 Bills defenders not being on an NFL roster today indicates?

title: Buffalo Bills super fandom: How could I not make a jetpack?
summary: Look, I know. This whole thing is dragging out. If I had been more focused this would have been done in May or June I bet. Here we are with Summer basically over and I have major components of the armor still missing. It might be a relief at least to know that a large […]
full_text: Look, I know. This whole thing is dragging out. If I had been more focused this would have been done in May or June I bet. Here we are with Summer basically over and I have major components of the armor still missing. It might be a relief at least to know that a large part of the delay was due to stretch goals. I hemmed and hawed about making a jetpack for my already overly complicated project but eventually settled on hawed. Or is it hemmed? Whichever one means I built the jetpack. Jetpack – Complete with fuel Everything has to start with an endpoint concept and when making a jetpack, the idea should always be to take flight. That said, I’m not a rocket scientist and even the best rocket scientists haven’t built jetpacks like the ones we see in Star Wars . So what chance did I have? It turns out I had a decent idea on how to at least metaphorically take flight with this. Make it a true tailgate accessory. You got it. It’s not just a jetpack, it’s a snack pack that allows you to fuel up for gameday. Let’s talk process. Shaping plastic is certainly feasible, but whenever possible shortcuts are a good idea. I felt that attaching some radiator style funnels to some old cleaning wipe containers would look decently like rockets once painted. A central canister of laundry pods seemed like a good fit too. So before I show you the rest and how my jet/snack/pack will fling me up and gain some elevation to wipe the floor with tailgating, a warning is in order. The plastic itself on these is of a type that CAN be considered food safe. That said, when used to store cleaning products the plastic will leach chemicals and perfume into it. I spent far more time trying to sanitize these to make them safe than I did with painting and assembly combined. Even then there’s a faint scent I couldn’t get out. In other words, if you’re so impressed with this that you want to make your own or pay me exorbitant sums of money to make you a custom one, I can’t in good faith say it’s truly a wise idea to use it for food storage. Like I’m clearly about to show you I did. But you shouldn’t. Here’s what it looks like painted with the pewter paint I used to get my beskar look… That looks pretty cool doesn’t it? That’s the back of the pods container because the handle dealy-bops looked pretty neat and add some character. For the paint, I dind’t want to go too far overboard since this will connect to the backplate and should match the breastplate. So I did a similar “cosmic” look to the one from the breastplate. I went with a straight color on the lids so it’s obvious they’re lids. Now when it comes to structure, I had a dilemma on my hands. The wipes containers were easy to join to the pods container with the Chicago/screw rivets I used elsewhere. The funnels I couldn’t really do that with. Soda bottle came to the rescue! It turns out bottle caps from soda bottles fit into the funnel end and wedge in nicely. I screwed a hole in the caps and in the canisters and used a thin bolt to pull the cap toward the canister and snug it up to the wipes container. Here’s the final look: We’re not quite done yet though. I promised fuel and I meant both food for energy and some “rocket fuel.” Obligatory disclaimer that you must be 21 or older to drink and even so, please drink responsibly. You should probably be reasonable about how many snack cakes, meat sticks, and cheese and cracker packs you consume too.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 7 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 17: Greg Olsen #88 of the Carolina Panthers after their game against the Atlanta Falcons at Bank of America Stadium on November 17, 2019 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Jacob Kupferman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #7. Greg Olsen If this countdown was ranking trades in Carolina Panthers history, Greg Olsen would be number one, and it wouldn’t be close. Olsen came into the NFL via Miami as a late first round pick of the Chicago Bears. He steadily rose to prominence over the course of his first three seasons before the Bears hired Mike Martz to be their offensive coordinator between Olsen’s third and fourth seasons. Martz’s offense heavily deemphasized the tight end position compared to the offenses that Olsen was starting to thrive in, and Olsen’s production dramatically fell off because of that. Deciding his services were no longer required, the Bears traded Olsen to the Panthers in 2011 for a third round pick. Olsen joined veteran Jeremy Shockey to form an elite tight end duo in support of rookie quarterback Cam Netwon. Olsen didn’t quite bounce back to his earlier production due to the split duties and the relatively low passing volume under a rookie quarterback. Shockey departed after that season, and that allowed Olsen to ascend to the level of elite tight ends. Olsen topped 800 yards in each of his first two seasons as the team’s cut and dry TE1. He would only continue to go up. Olsen topped 1,000 yards in 2014, 2015, and 2016, becoming the first tight end in NFL history to tally over 1,000 yards receiving in three straight seasons. He was the leading receiver on the 2015 team that went to the Super Bowl after a 15-1 regular season. With the Panthers in a constant struggle to acquire wide receiver talent, Olsen stayed constant as Cam Newton’s favorite and most reliable target. Unfortunately, Olsen’s peak would come to a rather abrupt end as his 2017 and 2018 seasons were derailed by recurring problems with his foot. He was able to get healthy for the 2019 season, but at age 34 and coming off two years full of foot problems, he wasn’t the same player. He finished that year with just 597 yards receiving and two touchdowns. The Panthers released him after that season. He spent one year with the Seahawks before calling it a career. Olsen is very visible in the media world now. For my money, he’s the best color commentator on TV working for FOX. He also has a podcast focusing on youth sports, and he and George Kittle run a camp for NFL tight ends every summer. He’s about as visible a Panther as there is in sports media. Olsen currently sits third in catches and receiving yards and fourth in receiving touchdowns in the history of the Panthers. He’s got the second best tight end in catches and yards (Wesley Walls) beat by 200 catches and over 2,500 yards. He’s the best tight end in franchise history, and he lands at number seven on our countdown of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 8 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - DECEMBER 01: Jordan Gross #69 of the Carolina Panthers during their game at Bank of America Stadium on December 1, 2013 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #8. Jordan Gross A lot of people who know football will tell you that outside of quarterback, a franchise left tackle is the most important and hardest position to lock in on an offense. The Panthers had that all through the 200s and into the 2010s with Jordan Gross. Gross’s early sports playing days are very typical of good offensive linemen. He’s from a rural state (Idaho), was a three sport athlete in high school, and was elite at all three sports. He was best at football, which earned him a scholarship to Utah, where he developed into an All American by his senior season. He built up enough of a resume to be selected with the eighth overall pick in the 2003 NFL Draft; he was the first offensive linemen off the board. Gross immediately provided return on that investment by starting at right tackle out of the gate. He played every offensive snap in his rookie season and established himself as an above average tackle right away. He would alternate between right tackle and left tackle each season for the first six years of his career, and it wasn’t until his sixth year that he would miss a start. In that season, he starred an offensive line that helped the Panthers to a top 10 offense despite being almost entirely built around the run game. He earned Pro Bowl and All Pro honors for his work that season. He would go on to earn two more Pro Bowl nominations while starting nearly every game for the Panthers over the next five seasons. He was as steady as could be throughout those years, even earning one of those Pro Bowl nominations in his final professional season in 2013. In all, Gross played in 167 games across his 11 year career in Carolina, starting every one of them. He was above average at his worst and elite at his best. Having that at left tackle for over a decade is something every team dreams of. In some ways, the Panthers have been continually trying to replace Gross since his retirement over 12 years ago. After his playing career came to a close, Gross stayed close to the organization, working as a sideline reporter for preseason games and hosting a Panthers-centric TV show with former teammate Travelle Wharton. He’s since returned home to coach football at his old high school and is now the offensive line coach at his alma mater. Gross’s 167 starts are the most in franchise history, and he has earned himself a spot in the Panthers Hall of Honor. His longevity, ability, and closeness to the franchise also earn him a spot at number eight on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

Before we get down to the nitty-gritty, a reminder to please subscribe to our podcast feed wherever you get your audio and leave us a review and/or a rating. Also, subscribe to our YouTube channel. Subscriptions, likes, and reviews help their algorithms put our brand in front of more people. So we could use your help! Our schedule is based on Sunday games, and the Bears currently have 10, so our lineup will change when they play on a different day of the week. *All listed times are Central* MONDAY 6:00 p.m. Livestream Video: Bear & Balanced from Jeff “JB” Berckes and Lester A. Wiltfong Jr. is their day-after, cooled-down postgame take of the Bears game. The fellas run a tight show as they work through their usual weekly segments, which always start with the linemen and their Trench Tribute, and end with the only porridge-themed segment in all of podcasting. They always try to stick around after for some video-exclusive Q&A with Bears fans. So hang out with us before the Monday Night Football game each week. PM Podcast: As soon as the Bear & Balanced video ends, we’ll quickly cut it up and publish the show to our podcast channel. TUESDAY Podcast/Video: Bill Zimmerman’s Bears Banter features a weekly guest drawn from his decades of experience in sports media. Since Bill will work around his guests’ busy schedules to ensure he has the best content possible for our fans each week, his show may occasionally be published at different times. Bill will also have his Bears Banter published on our 2nd City Gridiron video channel each week, so stay tuned and turn those notifications on so you never miss his premiere. WEDNESDAY 8:00 p.m. Livestream Video: Hang out with hosts Ryan Droste and Bryan Orenchuk, who are back again for another season of Bears Over Beers . Bears Over Beers is once again our weekly pivot show, and we want you guys to drive the discussion. Ryan and Bryan will kick off each show featuring a tasty beverage before settling in to talk about the previous game, the upcoming game, and anything else you want to discuss. So pull up a stool and bring your favorite drink for a laid-back, interactive chat about the Bears live on our YouTube channel! PM Podcast: If you missed the livestream of Bears Over Beers , you can catch the audio version as soon as the fellas publish it on our podcast feed. THURSDAY 6:00 p.m. Livestream Video: The Mac & Read Show from Evan McLean and Ross Read returns for year two! These two lifelong Chicago sports fans will look ahead to the game; they may also get into the other Windy City teams, plus they’ll also talk music, pop culture, food, current events, and so much more. PM Podcast: As soon as The M ac & Read Show ends on the video feed, we’ll chop it up and publish the show to our podcast channel. FRIDAY Podcast/Video: Taylor Doll’s Making Monsters is our game preview show. Each week, she’ll call up a guest (thanks to her massive Rolodex of media contacts) with ties to the Bears’ upcoming opponent, and they break down what to expect for each game. She’ll also have a segment with a Bears analyst to chop it up about all the latest on our favorite team. Her fantastic Making Monsters segment spotlighting Chicago players will still be there occasionally, so stay tuned to see which family member, former coach, or media member she finds to share some insight on our favorite Bears. Taylor’s podcast will usually show up on Friday mornings, with the video version dropping early that evening. SATURDAY 10:00 a.m. Livestream Video: How about some Bears for Breakfast with Jacob Infante and Jacob White? Bears for Breakfast is brand new to our lineup, and we couldn’t be more excited to see what Jacob and Jacob (2 Jakes, wow!) come up with each week. They’ll discuss the upcoming Bears game, go over the final game day injury report, do a little fantasy football talk, and touch on some of the draft prospects the Bears could have their eyes on. SUNDAY We don’t have a regularly scheduled immediate postgame show this season; however, someone on our team may have time on occasion to jump on the mic, so subscribe to our YouTube page and turn on notifications so you know when we go live. And if you need that postgame fix, then join us on Mondays for Bear & Balanced! During the week, we may have an occasional Bearly a Podcast pop up if there is important breaking news about the Bears. We’ll also have YouTube Shorts and occasional Xs & Os content, so if you subscribe, you’ll never miss a thing. HOST BIOS Jeff “JB” Berckes: Jeff serves as the Assistant Editor for Windy City Gridiron and podcast co-host for Bear & Balanced and multiple limited series shows. Jeff runs half marathons (over 60 finishes in 45 states to date) and loves to travel, eat the local fare, and drink new and interesting libations. He and Lester independently own the 2nd City Gridiron network. Taylor Doll: Taylor has been covering the NFL to some extent since 2015, when she began her internship at 1010XL, the flagship station of the Jacksonville Jaguars. In addition to her weekly podcast, she is the social media director, sports update reporter, and co-host of Helmets & Heels on 1010XL. But as a lifelong Bears fan, she brings her passion as the host of Making Monsters for 2nd City Gridiron. Ryan Droste: Ryan is a lifelong Bears fan and contributor to Windy City Gridiron. He has covered sports and entertainment extensively, with bylines at Sports Illustrated, CBS Interactive, Entrepreneur, and many others. Ryan is also the founder and host of Top Rope Nation, a professional wrestling podcast, and for you history buffs, be sure to check out his Substack, History Beyond The Bell . It’s 5 o’clock somewhere, so crack open a cold one and join Ryan on Bears Over Beers. Bryan Orenchuk: Bryan played his high school and college football in Florida, where he was a walk-on Running Back at the University of Central Florida and competed in multiple National Flag Football Tournaments before getting into rugby. After his playing days, Bryan coached middle school football for five years. He became a WCG contributor in 2024 and is a co-host of Bears Over Beers , with fellow Girl-Dad, Ryan Droste. Evan McLean & Ross Read: Evan and Ross are good friends who have been talking sports on air in Chicago together for the better part of a decade now. Come for the unique football content, and stay for breakdowns of your favorite shows, movies, pop culture, and Hip Hop projects. The Mac & Read Show is just like 2013 Matt Forte; there’s nothing these guys can’t do. Jacob Infante: Jacob is the lead draft analyst for Windy City Gridiron and the Director of Media Partnerships for Pro Football Network. He has covered the Bears and the NFL Draft for WCG since 2017, specializing in scouting reports, player interviews, and film reviews. He covers the NFL as a whole for PFN. He has been featured on outlets including Barstool Sports, USA Today, NBC5 Chicago, WGN, NewsNation, 670 The Score, WLS 890, Bleacher Report, SB Nation, and more. Jacob has had a podcast presence on our network for years, but now he’s debuting a brand-new show, Bears for Breakfast ! Jacob White: Jacob White is a co-host of Bears for Breakfast and a lifelong Chicago Bears fan. His interest in football began through the statistical side of the game, eventually leading him to work as a fantasy football writer for Gridiron Experts and FantasyPros, where he was also an expert ranker. He graduated from Wabash College in 2025 with a degree in economics and now lives and works in downtown Chicago in the insurance industry. Jacob prides himself on bringing a quintessential Gen Z approach to football, keeping things casual and humorous while maintaining a sharp eye for the numbers and strategy that dictate the game. title: Bears fans optimistic about the offseason, but still concerned about the d-line
summary: We asked Chicago Bears fans earlier this week to grade Chicago’s entire offseason. From free agency to the draft, to training camp performances, to preseason, and everything in between. Nearly half of us gave it a B, but the prevailing thought in our comments was concern about the defensive line. There wasn’t a big free-agent […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - DECEMBER 14: Montez Sweat #98 high fives Gervon Dexter Sr. #99 of the Chicago Bears after a sack during the third quarter against the Cleveland Browns at Soldier Field on December 14, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images We asked Chicago Bears fans earlier this week to grade Chicago’s entire offseason. From free agency to the draft, to training camp performances, to preseason, and everything in between. Nearly half of us gave it a B, but the prevailing thought in our comments was concern about the defensive line. There wasn’t a big free-agent addition on the defensive line. A trade never materialized. The NFL Draft didn’t bring anyone on the first two days. And neither the secondary free-agent market nor cut-down day brought anything more than a 30-year-old who’ll start the season on the practice squad. Then they traded away their most productive defensive tackle from 2025. “I gave a B, but it’s really just an incomplete,” wrote DontDeserveDITKA. “Time will tell if areas of concern are addressed. If Booker, van den Berg, Lynch and the D line pan out I could go higher.” “I have seen nothing in the preseason that makes me glad we went safety at 1 versus DT/Edge,” wrote meathead66. “The championship window is shorter now, and he (Ryan Poles) did virtually nothing to improve the pass rush,” propheteer wrote. “Building the defense from the back to the front is astonishing.” Roman F said, “To me, the assignment was to fix the DL or at least get started on it.” Chicago’s offense is primed to take a step and be a top-5 unit, but the defense has some question marks. They brought in more scheme-specific fits for Dennis Allen, but they’ll have to overcome the Coby Bryant injury at safety, figure out who will rush the passer, and then there’s the Kyler Gordon saga. Our friends at FanDuel Sportsbook have 57 players listed with Defensive Player of the Year odds before getting to the first Bear, cornerback Jaylon Johnson at +12,500. Defensive end Montez Sweat is further down the board at +22,500, and the only other Chicago player listed is linebacker Devin Bush at +50,000. Those three will need to lead the defense, but they’ll need help to match the low rankings the 2025 group had. It seems like the Bears could be in a lot of shootouts, which makes sprinkling a little something on Caleb Williams for MVP at +1400 a fun and calculated risk.

I still question how much improvement we will see from the Patriots heading into year two for their new regime. The one indisputable fact is they have a legit star in A.J. Brown. And he’s primed to feast as Drake Maye’s top target. Lester A. Wiltfong Jr.: Jahmyr Gibbs is such a dynamic player, and if his usage increases as expected, he should win Detroit’s first OPOTY award since 1997. Jeff Berckes: I think the Bengals offense could be primed for a monster season, and JaMarr Chase has a shot to do some insane things with a healthy Joe Burrow. Big-time player on a team looking to do some damage; I think he’ll put up his best season to date (and I have no shares in fantasy…). Superfans: Can Caleb Williams pull the daily double and win MVP and Offensive Player of the Year? The last time it happened in the NFL was 2018, when Pat Mahomes went over five thousand passing yards and threw for 50 touchdowns. So with a bar that low, there’s no doubt the Iceman shall take all the hardware. Who is your pick for 2026 Offensive Player of the Year?

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: Who goes over 1,000 receiving yards this year?
summary: Ben Johnson has said he wants the Chicago Bears offense to be the highest-scoring of all-time. That’s obviously a bold goal, and if we are being honest, probably not one the Bears will hit this year. Don’t get me wrong, I expect the Bears offense to be excellent. I expect it to be a top […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 28: Luther Burden III #10 of the Chicago Bears catches a pass for a touchdown against the San Francisco 49ers during the first quarter of the game at Levi's Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ben Johnson has said he wants the Chicago Bears offense to be the highest-scoring of all-time. That’s obviously a bold goal, and if we are being honest, probably not one the Bears will hit this year. Don’t get me wrong, I expect the Bears offense to be excellent. I expect it to be a top 5 offense in the league. But being the greatest of all-time is something that will, more likely than not, not happen. But that’s okay; it’s going to be a really fun season watching this offense and seeing what Caleb Williams can do in the passing game. But that makes you think, if this Bears offense is as explosive as Ben Johnson thinks it can be, that would certainly mean that the passing yardage is going to be higher than we’ve ever seen in Chicago. This certainly feels like the season a healthy Caleb Williams would become the first Bears QB to surpass 4,000 yards passing, and if he does, we know that means 4,000+ receiving yards on the other side of the ball. That leads us to today’s question. What players will have over 1,000 yards receiving this year? This makes for a fun debate. We all love Jahdae Walker, but I think even the biggest Walker fans understand that he’s not going north of 1,000 yards. Neither is Kalif Raymond. Neither is Cole Kmet. The Bears have three players capable of going over 1,000 yards: Luther Burden, Rome Odunze, and Colston Loveland. Which ones go over? Is it all three? Answer: As long as the receiving core is relatively healthy, I think you can definitely make an argument that any of the three can do it. I will start with Rome Odunze. I think Rome falls short of the 1,000-yard line. I think he’s a key part of the offense, but I think he falls more into a secondary role this year amongst this trio and probably ends up around 800 yards or so. Last year, Loveland had 713 yards receiving. Most of those came over the last 12 games of the season, and if you average his numbers over those 12 games and project them to 17, that number actually jumps to 930. So does that mean Loveland goes over 1,000 yards? If he plays 17 games, I think he absolutely does. But I do have a hunch that Loveland misses just a couple of games. If that’s the case and he plays like 15 games, I think he ends up coming up just short and has about 950 yards or so on the season. That leaves Luther Burden, and that’s where things change. I think Burden does, in fact, become the explosive playmaker this team has needed, and he is the guy that goes over 1,000 yards on the season. I think it won’t be like 1500 yards, but I do think he gets somewhere around 1100 yards. So while three players are capable of going over 1000 yards, I think Burden is the only one. That isn’t being pessimistic; that’s being optimistic about the rest of the weapons. If my yardage guesses are correct, those three tally about 2850 total receiving yards. Let’s say Raymond and Kmet each get about 400 yards. If Walker gets around 300 yards, Swift gets around 250 yards. Sam Roush and Savion Thomas each just get 200 yards; that’s 4700 passing yards! This isn’t the Cincinnati Bengals with Chase and Higgins and not much else. The Bears have a lot of talented skill players on offense, and because of it, Burden is the only guy who will go north of 1,000 yards. What do you say, Bears fans? Do you agree? How many players get 1000 yards this season? Sound off in the comments below!
