Eason put too much good film on tape during preseason, which made it seem like he’d be worth developing. Willis had a couple of impressive blocks, but on a down-to-down basis, it was unlikely that he was going to contribute in any fashion. The 49ers used Willis on special teams during the preseason, perhaps to see how he’d fare. He did not register a solo tackle on 32 snaps. And with Kyle Juszczyk practicing and George Kittle returning, Willis wasn’t going to step onto the field. But you also have to factor in the roster dynamics. title: Lynch: ‘We didn’t foresee tendonitis” with Nick Bosa ACL injury
summary: The San Francisco 49ers are less than one week out from their season opener against the Los Angeles Rams, and they’ve already touched down in Australia as they adjust to the major time change before the game. The 49ers have been dealing with a ton of injuries ahead of the season, recently placing Sam Okuayinonu […]
full_text: May 3, 2019; Santa Clara, CA, USA; San Francisco 49ers defensive lineman Nick Bosa (97) warms up before practice during rookie minicamp at SAP Performance Facility. Mandatory Credit: Stan Szeto-USA TODAY Sports The San Francisco 49ers are less than one week out from their season opener against the Los Angeles Rams, and they’ve already touched down in Australia as they adjust to the major time change before the game. The 49ers have been dealing with a ton of injuries ahead of the season, recently placing Sam Okuayinonu on Injured Reserve, but they are expected to have Nick Bosa and George Kittle available in Week 1, with both making the trip to Australia. Bosa finally practiced in full for the first time this offseason earlier this week, as he’s made his recovery from an ACL tear and then tendonitis that unexpectedly popped up this summer, raising concerns. Speaking to the media, the defensive end acknowledged the difficulties with the recovery process and why the setback occurred. “It was a long road,” Bosa acknowledged. “There’s some stuff I dealt with, with that patellar tendon, and then I kind of ramped it a little too fast with the football stuff a month ago or whatever it was. And that kind of told me to back off. I’ve just been trying to get it as strong and as confident as I can to where I could rip the Band-Aid off and go to team stuff today. “Once you get into team, there’s no reservations, there’s no compensation … like there’s no governor,” Bosa said, via ESPN’s Nick Wagoner. “I felt that today. I remember my last ACL; there was a couple moments where you just have to go and you’re kind of hoping for the best. Obviously, it’s not going to be like anything crazy is going to happen, but you hope that your body is going to respond the way that you prepared it to. And there’s a couple moments today where that happened. So, I’m just going to try and keep building, not get too up about it, but it was a great day.” Speaking on The TK Show ahead of the Australia trip, general manager John Lynch spoke on both Bosa and Kittle’s recoveries, noting the expectation that both should make the trip and play. “Yeah, I think that’s fair to say, and the expectation is that they both are,” Lynch said when asked if both were making the trip and playing in Week 1. “They both have been tracking very well. Now, as we’ve said many times, ideal, no, but I think given the circumstances, we feel very good about where they’re at. “Big day for Nick today. He’s getting out on the practice field doing reps. That day was yesterday for George. George performed very well. His rehab has been outstanding, as has Nick’s. Nick just, you know, people at different times during ACLs, it’s kind of the norm. Nick is, I think we all know, blessed genetically, and I think in his other ACLs, hasn’t had this hiccup. And, you know, I call it a hiccup, but most guys go through it and they get a little tendonitis. You have to back off. We didn’t foresee that with Nick, but it happened. And so you adjust accordingly and feel very good about his ability. He trains so diligently. I think he’s ready, and we’ll see. Provided everything goes well here today, we’ll expect Nick to be in uniform and making the impact he always does against the Rams.” Even if they unexpectedly don’t suit up in Week 1, having both around the team was important for the organization, given how much time the 49ers are spending in Australia. “Absolutely, [it’s important for them to make the trip],” Lynch added. “I mean, there’s certain guys who I always look over, and when you’re coming off the field, there’s Trent Williams, there’s Kittle, there’s Nick, Deebo gives you that sense. A lot of these players give you that sense, man. All right, this is pretty cool. And we’ve got a number of them. Mike Evans, we add to the mix. We’ve got a lot of top-end players, and we’re fortunate to have that. Guys that will be in the conversation for Hall of Fame later after their careers are over, and they’ve earned that. And yeah, it is comforting, and it’s comforting for teammates as well.” We’ll see how much both players see the field in Week 1, as it’d make sense for both to be on a pitch count as they ramp up. But it’s a good sign that the 49ers key injuries are starting to trend in the right direction ahead of Week 1.

title: Where would you rank the Kyle Shanahan/Brock Purdy duo in the NFL?
summary: We can have all sorts of Brock Purdy arguments at any time. If there’s one thing we can all agree needs improvement, it’s his durability. We’re still trying to see him play his second full NFL season (he missed the last game of 2023 because the 49ers had the first seed in the playoffs locked […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 21: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers stands on the field with head coach Kyle Shanahan prior to an NFL football game against the Arizona Cardinals at Levi's Stadium on September 21, 2025 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We can have all sorts of Brock Purdy arguments at any time. If there’s one thing we can all agree needs improvement, it’s his durability. We’re still trying to see him play his second full NFL season (he missed the last game of 2023 because the 49ers had the first seed in the playoffs locked up) Over at CBS Sports, Garrett Podell ranked the top head coach-quarterback duos heading into the 2026 season. He has Brock Purdy and Kyle Shanahan at sixth. As should surprise no one, the Los Angeles Rams’ Sean McVay and Matthew Stafford ranked ahead of them. As something that should surprise everyone, the McVay/Stafford duo ranked first, while the Patrick Mahomes/Andy Reid tandem from the Kansas City Chiefs ranked second. Purdy/Shanahan also fell behind their other NFC West rivals, the Seattle Seahawks, with Sam Darnold and Mike MacDonald (third). Here’s what Podell said about the Purdy/Shanahan connection: Despite the San Francisco 49ers’ top-six highest-paid players missing a league-leading 64 games (including the postseason), they made the playoffs and won a road playoff game at the Philadelphia Eagles. That’s an impressive feat for the 49ers’ duo of quarterback Brock Purdy and head coach Kyle Shanahan. Purdy’s situational efficiency in Shanahan’s scheme reached new heights in 2025 with him completing 58.3% of his third and fourth down pass attempts, the highest rate by any quarterback in the last 35 seasons, per CBS Sports Research. Like the rest of the San Francisco roster, Purdy needs to work on improving his durability. He missed a combined 11 games across the last three seasons, including eight in 2025 with a turf toe injury. Shanahan is a master at maximizing whoever is on the football field, but it would be nice to see him work with a full deck for once. That may be difficult with much of his core on the wrong side of 30. As we said to start this, it’s safe to say we can all agree Purdy needs to be more durable. In his rookie season, after tearing up his elbow, everyone said he wasn’t durable after one (1) injury. The very next season, with concussions, big hits, etc., he started every game (except the last one, since the 49ers were the first seed and didn’t need to play their starters). Even though he started every game, he got banged up a lot (so much that he had to be yanked for a play or two in some games to get checked by the training staff). 2024 had some moments without him, and the 2025 turf toe injury kept him deficient in some games at best and out of them completely at worst. A deficient Purdy isn’t the worst thing, but ask the Jacksonville Jaguars, and they will tell you it is far from ideal. Aside from his durability, Purdy has shown with Shanahan that he is a top-10 quarterback. We need to see him stay in games. Still, sixth in the coach/quarterback duo seems a bit high. I thought the whole reason Purdy was good was Shanahan. I thought Shanahan’s career was saved after drafting Brock Purdy when the Trey Lance failure became apparent. As Podell mentions, some may question MacDonald/Darnold at third—I’m one of them. It seemed like MacDonald was doing a majority of the heavy lifting last year with that defense and running game. That said, Sam Darnold has a Super Bowl ring, and Brock Purdy does not. Take from that what you will. Where would you put the Shanahan/Purdy duo in the NFL?

Daniels wasn’t healthy and started just seven games. They were 31st in turnover EPA. They were 30th in AGL , which measures which teams were most hurt by injuries. And they were 1-5 in games decided by seven points or fewer. As mentioned above with the Eagles, turnover luck, injury luck, and performances in close games are not typically things that carry over from one year to the next. The 2025 Commanders got quite unlucky with those things. Perhaps the 2026 Commanders will land more around league average in those categories. If Daniels regains the magic from his rookie season, that will give Washington its most direct path to a playoff berth. Last year, he ranked 25th in EPA per pass play and 15th in success rate among 37 qualifying quarterbacks. The difference in the two numbers suggests that Daniels was slightly above average down to down, but he got dinged by turnovers and a lack of explosive plays. Like the Eagles, the Commanders appear to be implementing a massive offensive scheme change, going from Kliff Kingsbury to David Blough. Blough has just two years of coaching experience and will be calling plays for the first time. The expectation is that Washington will implement more under-center, play-action schemes, as opposed to Kingsbury’s shotgun, up-tempo spread attack. The scheme change on defense also appears to be significant. Quinn hired Daronte Jones from Minnesota, and he is expected to employ a creative Brian Flores–style attack with heavy blitzing to make up for roster deficiencies. Jones has an intriguing background, but like Blough, he has never been an NFL coordinator before. In addition to the scheme change, the Commanders overhauled their personnel, adding edge defenders Odafe Oweh and K’Lavon Chaisson in free agency and drafting linebacker Sonny Styles seventh. If Jones proves to be a capable schemer, there are some pieces to work with here. The overhaul is real. Between the coaching staff and players, this is a completely different group, so drawing comparisons to the 2025 unit makes little sense. While the optimism is warranted, we must also understand that new defensive schemes don’t manifest into greatness overnight. There is an expected learning curve when a new coach shows up. A new philosophy with an influx of new components opens the door for communication breakdowns and blown assignments. The whole point of bringing Christian Parker in was to alleviate this, but there is no guarantee that it will work, and there’s a reasonable chance they’ll experience the typical…

title: Commanders debate: How secure is Washington coach Dan Quinn’s job status?
summary: I started writing an analysis on Sunday morning stating that Commanders head coach Dan Quinn’s job status is in some jeopardy — I despise the term “hot seat” — before ever playing a meaningful 2026 snap. And that rough overall record should prompt his ouster after a third season in Washington.   I had a […]
full_text: I started writing an analysis on Sunday morning stating that Commanders head coach Dan Quinn ’s job status is in some jeopardy — I despise the term “hot seat” — before ever playing a meaningful 2026 snap. And that rough overall record should prompt his ouster after a third season in Washington. I had a case laid out. It was debatable, but the logic was sound. Then my brain started messing with me. The deeper I got into the story, the more my inner voice started arguing with what was already written. I stared at it for a while. I read it and re-read it. Then I hit delete. The more I think about it, the Dan Quinn situation is nuanced, certainly not open-and-shut, and deserves to be treated as such. That’s why we’re taking it to the HH community. This is now a discussion post where we can debate this thing out. I don’t expect an eventual agreement or even a consensus. Just a (hopefully) rational conversation about Quinn, his role in the past two seasons and what expectations for him should be as we move into a crucial regular season for the franchise. The Commanders went 12-5 and reached the NFC title game in his first year. They went 5-12 in an injury-riddled campaign that showed Washington was too thin overall, and too old and slow defensively. Does he deserve all the credit for 2024? Nope. Does he deserve all the blame for 2025? Surely not. Now we’re entering Quinn’s third season, typically a defining year for modern NFL coaches, where teams expect to see a green arrow pointing way up. He’s obviously sticking around if Washington reaches the playoffs or simply finishes above .500. That would be a four-win improvement over last year and a sign Washington’s headed in the right direction. Let’s say, for this argument, this Commanders season goes the other way but not downright awful. Heads will obviously roll if the Commanders win just five (or less) games again. No way owner Josh Harris tolerates that. What if the improvement’s minimal? Is it all about wins and losses, or is the eye test part of all this? Quinn’s chiefly responsible for Commanders team culture. He’s responsible for player development and coaching development. He’s responsible for game management. If we see red flags there, that’s trouble. If there are talent and depth issues, is that on Quinn? See what I’m saying here? Nuanced. So, let’s go over a few scenarios here. If the Commanders are in that 6-8 win range, what do you do? Let D Q go There’s a push to find the next great play caller, pay him a ton and let him develop a young quarterback. The trend started with Sean McVay (or maybe Andy Reid) and has been present since. The 49ers got Kyle Shanahan. The Bears got Ben Johnson. Say what you want about his bedside manner, but the Jags got Liam Coen. If you want someone like that, the record won’t matter as much. Quinn’s of a different mold, a CEO-type coach and organizational leader. There are places where that works, namely with Dan Campbell in Detroit or Mike Vrabel in New England. If the organization wants a different type of coach, Quinn’s probably gotta go. Also, how does quarterback Jayden Daniels look? If he’s frustrated or seemingly held back by the system, then you’ve got a problem. If the team gives up on the staff and we see lopsided losses down the stretch, that’s another troubling indicator. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Keep DQ around To borrow a tired analogy (sorry), Quinn’s responsible for making the meal but he didn’t buy the ingredients. Injuries are tough, but there are four Peters-era second-round draft picks who aren’t yet misses but haven’t done much. It made sense after 2024 to let it ride and try to keep a good thing going, but that didn’t work and require more wholesale changes this offseason that may require time (and another NFL draft class) to produce dividends. Also, Quinn hired two new coordinators this offseason. Daronte Jones was brought in to run a system not based in Quinn’s. David Blough was promoted to run a more modern, less gimmicky NFL offensive attack. That was a bold move with two young play callers and they deserve time to develop systems and add talent that fits them. Firing Quinn likely means canning Blough and Jones and then you’re starting over again. And handing Daniels a third new offense in four NFL seasons. Not ideal for such a talent. Stay the course, understand this 2026 offseason was the start of something new that needs time to work out. That’s my pros and cons list. Where do you stand? What’s the right answer for the head coach position should Washington struggle somewhat in 2026? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Commanders fan anxiety spikes over O-Line skill & depth – survey results
summary: Fans are concerned As the Washington Commanders prepare to kick off the 2026 NFL campaign, the collective mood of the fan base is suspended somewhere between fragile optimism and overwhelming anxiety. In this week’s Reacts poll conducted by Hogs Haven, readers were asked to pinpoint their primary concern regarding the team heading into the new […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - AUGUST 18: Nick Allegretti #67 of the Washington Commanders looks on from the sideline during the national anthem prior to an NFL preseason football game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Northwest Stadium on August 18, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fans are concerned As the Washington Commanders prepare to kick off the 2026 NFL campaign, the collective mood of the fan base is suspended somewhere between fragile optimism and overwhelming anxiety. In this week’s Reacts poll conducted by Hogs Haven, readers were asked to pinpoint their primary concern regarding the team heading into the new season. The results were overwhelmingly focused on one area: 65% of respondents stated that offensive line skill and depth is the biggest worry, while 11% identified the job done by general manager Adam Peters as their chief concern. By contrast, 9% of the fan base reported pure excitement for the new season, unburdened by dread of roster or other shortcomings. Visit our partners at FanDuel The interconnected anxiety about the roster & the front office On the surface, the low percentage of fans explicitly pointing their fingers at general manager Adam Peters might suggest a high level of trust for AP. However, constructing a football roster is a tightly woven ecosystem. It seems likely that the 11% who identify the GM as the primary concern are judging him largely through the lens of having failed to build an effective roster, with the offensive line featuring prominently in that negative assessment. In other words, the anxiety surrounding the front office and the anxiety surrounding the five men up front are largely the same conversation. The perceived failure of roster execution in his three years at the helm — and specifically this offseason — is where negative critiques of Peters tend to focus. A tale of two worries: The center and left tackle woes The fan base’s high anxiety revolves primarily around two glaring issues along the line – issues of very different origins. One was due to injury, which is part and parcel of the NFL, while the other appears to have been at least partly self-inflicted. 1. The self-inflicted center tempest The most scrutinized sequence of events this offseason started when the front office made the bold choice to cut Tyler Biadasz several days before the start of free agency. While moving on from a starter is not uncommon in the NFL, the subsequent plan (or failure of the plan) raised eyebrows. Peters failed to secure a definitive, high-tier upgrade at center through free agency or the early rounds of the draft. Instead, the front office handed the keys to veteran guard Nick Allegretti, banking on him to be a healthy, consistent starter – even now, despite a lingering calf injury that cost him nearly all of training camp. Exacerbating this gamble was the failure to secure a proven backup. Should Allegretti’s injury flare back up, the primary reinforcement is rookie sixth-round draft pick Matt Gulbin . Relying on a late-round rookie and an injured converted guard to solidify the interior protection appears to be a flashing red light for roughly two-thirds or three-quarters of our survey respondents. 2. The unavoidable hit at tackle The secondary crisis arose when star left tackle Laremy Tunsil suffered a torn triceps midway through training camp, an unavoidable and unfortunate injury that weakens both starter and backup at two positions — left tackle and left guard — entering the season. The critical differences between the two issues are that the tackle position was backed up with talented depth, and the trigger was an unavoidable injury. Looked at in one light, it actually indicates good roster planning. Things are very different with the depth chart for the center position, the avoidability of the precipitating event, and the roster approach of the front office. Proactive elsewhere, passive at center What makes the center situation so frustrating for the Hogs Haven community is that Adam Peters demonstrated proactivity at other positions. When roster holes or depth issues became apparent late in the summer, the front office took action: Brought in elite veteran wide receiver Stefon Diggs to bolster the receiver group. Secured veteran cornerbacks Rasul Douglas and Fabian Moreau to steady the secondary. Signed veteran tackle D.J. Humphries as veteran insurance behind Coleman. Yet, even as multiple centers were traded across the league in the hours leading up to final roster cutdowns, Washington chose to stand pat. The stakes: Protecting Jayden Daniels and executing David Blough’s scheme The consequences of this uneven roster construction could turn out to be a big deal when the regular season starts. Franchise quarterback Jayden Daniels must be kept clean to survive and thrive in his key 3 rd NFL season. Furthermore, newly promoted offensive coordinator David Blough —who is stepping into a major play-calling role for the first time—has promised a creative, high-speed offense designed to stress defenses. Neither Daniels’ health, nor Blough’s playbook, can thrive if the offensive line can’t hold up against quality defensive talent. This idea is scary when looking at the Commanders schedule . In the first half of the upcoming season alone, Washington must face some of the most destructive defensive lines and interior pass rushers in the NFL. The Commanders will have to match up against the division-rival Philadelphia Eagles’ bruising front, a re-made Cowboys defensive unit under new DC Christian Parker, the Seahawks Super Bowl-caliber defense, and a Houston Texans defense boasting an elite edge-and-interior combination. If a majority of the fan base is losing sleep as kickoff approaches, it’s not for nothing. The front office has upgraded the defense from front to back and added weapons for the offense led by Jayden Daniels, but it’s hard to feel confident that the offensive line – especially without Laremy Tunsil or a battle-tested center – will be up to the task. The case for optimism With all that said, the Commanders have not yet taken a single regular season snap. Everything is still in front of them, and, in many ways, the team appears deeper and stronger than the 2024 group that played in the NFC Championship game. Joe Whitt has been replaced at DC by Daronte Jones – known for his teaching skill and and history with an aggressively attacking scheme. The DL, pass rushers and linebacking groups have all had major infusions of talent this offseason, and the secondary may benefit from the improved coaching and scheme that Jones is expected to bring to Washington. Offensively, this may be the deepest and most talented group of wide receivers to play in Washington in at least a decade. A similar claim might be made about the tight end room, especially with respect to blocking ability. The running back group, while unheralded and without marquee name recognition, offers a mix of skills and styles that should be able to continue to produce the strong rushing metrics the Commanders put up under Dan Quinn in 2024 & 2025. Most of all, every Commanders fan should know about the magical play of Jayden Daniels. It may not have been on display much in 2025, but we all remember what he was able to do in his rookie year when he was mostly healthy and playing behind an offensive line that was not really any better than the one he will rely on vs the Eagles next week. JD5’s unique abilities, if he can avoid the kind of injuries that plagued him a year ago, erase a lot of mistakes and lift the play of every offensive player on the field with him. With Jayden Daniels, the Commanders go into every game with a chance to win. Season opener The Commanders will open their 2026 NFL regular season on the road as underdogs against their division rivals. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Sports Illustrated How an Injury-Plagued 2025 Can Help Jayden Daniels in the Long Run The Commanders’ starting QB and breakout star in 2024 is anxious to show the football world what he’s been working on for the past five months They will give Daniels more responsibility, and command at the line, which the quarterback himself thinks leans into one of his strengths. Learning a new system, with longer, more verbose calls and more variables before the snap, is one thing. But applying it is another, and the call-it periods, where Daniels couldn’t see what was coming on a script, were built to accelerate his ability to do that. Quinn also hired a Brian Flores disciple, Daronte Jones, to run a system that might be the NFL’s most complex, which only adds to how difficult the summer was going to be for Daniels. The response from Daniels? As the coaches saw it, he looked like a quarterback who couldn’t get enough of it, and wanted to be pushed the way he was. “I like the vibe that they create together”, [said Dan Quinn], “because they push one another in a way of, O.K., I don’t know if we can get all this , and, of course, Jayden is like, Put the play in, the protection in, everything . I like that they are hungry in that way together.” And the results, in the quarterback’s eyes, are already showing up. In a nutshell, he has more room to talk in the huddle. The reward? He has the autonomy to put his own twist on whatever the call is. Jayden Daniels on Commanders OC David Blough’s scheme: “The balance of play-action passes, the bootlegging, stuff that we’re able to run to marry up with our run game, get those guys moving laterally, it’s going to help out to be able to get some shots in to showcase what I can… pic.twitter.com/zVOlH1Ffvz — SleeperNFL (@SleeperNFL) September 4, 2026 The flexibility there, Daniels learned, extends to actually being able to change things on the fly—which, philosophically, should allow the Commanders to go to unscripted things right up until the snap, based on what the defense is showing the QB. The offense has a lot of answers baked in, and gives Daniels the latitude to come up with his own. Great nugget from the @AlbertBreer piece on Jayden Daniels via SI today. Apparently DQ shortened the play clock in practices. pic.twitter.com/q18peqWpH0 — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) September 4, 2026 “I’m getting more comfortable, where I might call a play and I know the final formation, but I might put a little shift or a motion on it beforehand, and [Blough] doesn’t know that I’m doing that,” he said. “So we break the huddle, and honestly, he’s thinking that we f—ed up; I might have called a play wrong. And he’s screaming, and I’m just giving him one of those— I got it . And he’s like, O.K., he’s got it. He’s doing his own little thing . “Honestly, how we look as an offense, I’m super excited to see how Blough can call a game,” Daniels said. “You get 60 plays in the game, so how he schemes up a lot of different things, because there are times where [Sean] McVay or the guys like Ben Johnson, KOC, they scheme people open based on what they’re watching and tendencies. So I’m excited for that.” Commanders QB Jayden Daniels is anxious to show the football world what he’s been working on for the past five months after an injury-plagued 2025, writes @AlbertBreer pic.twitter.com/wXcXF48WPw — Sports Illustrated (@SInow) September 4, 2026 To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Fast, Physical and Joyful: Inside Daronte Jones’ Vision for Commanders Defense Fast and physical can be considered buzzwords because they come up so often in conversations about pretty much any NFL defense, but Reaves included joy, which is a bit different and shows another layer of Jones’ vision for Washington. “He’s a very intelligent dude, very passionate guy. He loves ball, and he loves to teach football. The guys that are out there will love ball and will love to learn, and love to, you know, celebrate each other, not just themselves. That’s the genetic makeup of him.” Clearly, the desired identity Jones wants goes far beyond how the team plays physically; it focuses on how each player communicates and responds to the others. Another major offseason emphasis for Washington has been creating more takeaways. Rather than waiting for those opportunities, Reaves explained that the Commanders are trying to make attacking the football automatic. “We’ve programmed the subconscious to always think about the ball,” Reaves said. “We work drills every day, and we work things every day to where even if the whistle’s blown, right, we’re still punching at the ball. You never know when the ball is going to come out.” That repetition is designed to make defenders recognize the vulnerable moments an offensive player presents without having to stop and think about it. “Just always training your mind to go after it because there are vulnerable positions when the offense does have the ball, and we have to maximize those opportunities to take it off of them.” The approach fits directly into the fast and physical part of Jones’ identity. Playing aggressively is one thing, but doing it with purpose gives Washington a chance to turn tackles into game-changing possessions. So, the Commanders are doing everything they can to overcome that obstacle by getting comfortable with silent counts. “There’s a couple different ones that we use,” head coach Dan Quinn said. “So, just getting the reps at that. We’ve done some in the evenings and the walkthroughs and just more volume of it, honestly. Most teams like us have more than one that they use and so you can kinda lean into one. Now I need more work at the second one, but Nick’s experience really shows through on that.” The Commanders spent much of the offseason hyping up Allegretti’s intelligence and experience as the main reasons they’re giving him a chance at center. He’s spent most of his career at guard — 2,553 snaps, to be exact — but he feels like center is his natural position. The Commanders feel like his ability to make protection calls at the line of scrimmage will be a boon for the offensive line and raise the performance of the entire group. Allegretti believes he is ready for the challenge, even if it is against one of the best teams in the conference. “I feel really comfortable with Jayden,” Allegretti said. “I always communicated with him like I was a center, just because that’s who I am at my core … Happy to be back there. title: McBride, Wingard bury college grudge as safety joins Cardinals
summary: With college feud behind them, the Cardinals' No. 1 tight end and veteran safety are becoming fast friends.
full_text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- For seven years, four months and 18 days, Andrew Wingard held a grudge against  Trey McBride .

 It all started with a play that has faded into a distant memory. Few can recall the moment on that Oct. 26, 2018, night, when Colorado State and Wyoming played the 110th edition of their Border War rivalry. The way Wingard, a senior on that Cowboys team, tells it, he was on the ground after making a tackle when McBride, a Rams freshman tight end at the time, speared him in the back and kneed him in the ribs.

 Wingard took offense -- and then some.

 McBride, on the other hand, contests Wingard's account of the play.

 "I don't know about the spear in the back, things like that," said McBride, currently a star tight end for the  Arizona Cardinals . "It was just playing through the whistle, whatever it is.

 "Me and him got a little tangled up. It was unfortunate, but yes, he's held a grudge for a while."

 But McBride didn't realize how long Wingard held a grudge.

 "I knew he was frustrated at the play," McBride said. "The whole fanbase was mad at me, Wyoming. But like I said, it was such a long time ago. I honestly, it kind of spaced my mind.

 "And then as you see him throughout your years and you keep playing against him, you just kind of always go back to like, man, hopefully he forgot about it, and he never did."

 Wingard had chances to let it go, but he wouldn't. He carried it from the mountains of Fort Collins, Colorado, site of Saturday's 118th Border War, to the plains of Laramie, Wyoming, to the shores of Jacksonville, Florida, to cities around the NFL. After the two faced each other in November when Wingard was still playing for the Jaguars, McBride came over to Wingard to tell him he respected him. All Wingard could say in response was "F--- you." Looking back on it now, Wingard regrets that he didn't leave his feelings inside the white lines during the 60 minutes they played.

 But in March, Wingard finally released his grudge against McBride in the Arizona desert.

 It was time, Wingard felt. The two were no longer bitter college rivals. Wingard was signing with the Cardinals as a free agent, and they were going to be teammates. As fate would have it, the first person Wingard saw when he arrived at the Cardinals' practice facility in Arizona to sign his contract on March 16 was McBride.

 "It was kind of like the 'Step Brothers' moment where it was like, OK, I'm over it sort of thing," Wingard said of the 2008 Will Ferrell comedy. "And it was funny because he was the first guy I saw when I came in and signed my contract and it was just like, all right man. Yeah, I'm over it. I'm over it.

 "So, we're cool now."

 McBride thought the moment was funny.

 "We made eye contact and the first thing he said was, 'All right man, we can be friends now because we're teammates,'" McBride said. "So, it was just cool."

 Now, Wingard said, McBride is "one of my guys on the team."

 The two have come so far, and it only took a decade.

 However, those who knew McBride and Wingard in college weren't surprised by how either acted on the play and after.

 "I can tell both players had a similar personality trait of being ultracompetitive and somewhat edgy," former Wyoming coach Craig Bohl said. Bohl convinced McBride to take a recruiting trip to Wyoming as a high schooler but knew the chances of landing McBride were "slim and none" because McBride's older brother was already at Colorado State.

 "I can tell you, if the roles were reversed, I would say Trey would probably hold a grudge that long also."

 Former Colorado State tight end Cam Butler played alongside McBride for two seasons before missing the 2020 season with a foot injury, and said McBride was "great to play with."

 "He would be an awful person to play against because he just doesn't care," Butler said.

 Former Colorado State offensive coordinator Dave Johnson couldn't think of which scuffle it was that McBride got into it with Wingard. And for good reason. It wasn't that McBride had a short fuse, but if an opponent was "putting a little mustard on a player after a tackle," then McBride wouldn't put up with that, Johnson explained.

 "Trey was known to get into scuffles," Johnson said, "so it's a little difficult to pinpoint which one you're talking about, because he was apt to be involved in a couple things during the course of games."

 And the Border War just meant emotions ran even higher.

 The two schools are separated by just 62 miles, an exact distance Bohl quickly rattled off. Bohl said he always got along with the Colorado State head coaches but knew "a lot" of the opposing players "had some spark" between them because some had known each other, grew up with each other or played each other before they got to college.

 "The Border War, it was everything for those two schools," Butler said. "We didn't like them. They didn't like us. It was that kind of thing."

 The game is played for the Bronze Boot, a trophy the winning team has kept since its introduction in 1968. The pomp and circumstance for the long, heated rivalry goes beyond the game. On Friday, the day before the game, the Wyoming ROTC will hand the game ball off to the Colorado State ROTC, which will then carry the ball back to Fort Collins.

 "It goes back years and years and years across families," Bohl said. "You've got some families where one person went to CSU, the other person went to Wyoming, and so there's respect, but there's no love lost between the two."

 Butler remembered on the Monday of one of his Wyoming game weeks, former Rams running backs coach Bryan Applewhite stood in front of the offense and instead of going over stats, like he'd typically do in that weekly meeting, Applewhite pulled up a photo of Wingard with one specific instruction: Don't let him affect the game.

 "I know Trey some, I mean, he and [Wingard], if you put those two in a box, that's why they [were so] competitive,'" Bohl said. "They ain't going to be warm, fuzzy guys.

 "Now, they're probably going to be best of friends."

title: 2026 NFL rookies guide: Stat leaders, fantasy picks, top QBs
summary: Here's what to know about this group of rookies, including Rookie of the Year front-runners, fantasy favorites and QB updates.
full_text:
Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season will feature plenty of rookie debuts. Although No. 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza won't make an appearance for at least a few weeks, the rest of the top-five selections should have an early impact (Jets edge rusher  David Bailey , Cardinals running back  Jeremiyah Love , Titans receiver  Carnell Tate and Giants linebacker  Arvell Reese ). And there are plenty of non-first-rounders who have created preseason hype, including 49ers receiver De'Zhaun Stribling , Broncos running back Jonah Coleman  and Colts safety A.J. Haulcy .

 Which 2026 draft picks could have huge seasons? Who might contribute on your fantasy football roster? Here's our guide to everything you need to know about the rookie class.

 NFL draft analyst Jordan Reid and betting analyst Pamela Maldonado start by naming early Offensive and Defensive Rookie of the Year contenders (including their DraftKings odds to win). Then NFL analyst Matt Bowen picks five under-the-radar players to watch, national NFL reporter Dan Graziano gives notes on the rookie QBs, and fantasy analyst Eric Moody projects the top 10 rookie performers in fantasy. To cap it all off, we included Mike Clay's  projected rookie stat leaders .

 

 
 Jump to: 
 OROY candidates  | DROY candidates   
 Under-the-radar  | Fantasy picks 
 Quarterback notes  |  Projections 

 
 

 Reid's top Offensive Rookie of the Year candidates 
 

 1. Jeremiyah Love , RB, Arizona Cardinals  (+550) 
 Love became the first running back drafted in the top five since Saquon Barkley in 2018 (No. 2 overall). That obviously gives him high expectations, but he could meet them as the focal point of new coach Mike LaFleur's offense in Arizona.

 Love will not only contribute as a rusher but also as a pass catcher, where he can routinely take advantage of mismatches. In his lone preseason game against the Raiders, he showcased what he's capable of with 73 yards (58 rushing, 15 receiving) on 14 touches.

 
 

 2. Jadarian Price , RB, Seattle Seahawks  (+650) 
 Replacing reigning Super Bowl MVP   Kenneth Walker III won't be easy, but Price should bring a similar skill set to Seattle's offense. Where Price could bring more value, though, is in the passing game. Despite never surpassing double-digit receptions at Notre Dame, he showed plenty of comfort when asked to be an option out of the backfield.

 Price should also shine because of a  Brian Fleury offense featuring plays with two RBs and a mixture of downhill running concepts. His 3.96 yards after contact per rush ranked 25th among FBS rushers last season.

 
 

 3. Carnell Tate , WR, Tennessee Titans  (+600) 
 The No. 4 pick is expected to transform into a go-to target for second-year quarterback  Cam Ward . Tate is a diverse route runner who can execute routes at all levels of the field, but I expect him to stand out in the vertical passing game where he can accelerate past defenders. He averaged 17.2 yards per catch during his final season at Ohio State, which ranked seventh in the FBS among players with at least 50 receptions.

 
 

 

 4. De'Zhaun Stribling , WR, San Francisco 49ers  (+1100) 
 Stribling was a controversial pick at the top of the second round, but he had a strong preseason that included seven receptions in his first preseason game. And with  Ricky Pearsall  missing the entire season after knee surgery , Stribling should have an easier path to targets in coach Kyle Shanahan's system.

 A physical presence at 6-foot-2, 207 pounds, Stribling is also a detailed route runner who had 409 yards after the catch last season (33rd most in the FBS among all WRs). Shanahan is among the best coaches at glorifying the well-rounded skill sets of wideouts, and his work with Stribling should be no different.

 
 

 5. KC Concepcion , WR, Cleveland Browns  (+1800) 
 Concepcion is a sleeper candidate to win OROY because of the multiple ways he could shine as a rookie. He not only has inside-out versatility in new coach Todd Monken's offense, but he's also a dynamic returner who can create positive plays on special teams. In Year 1 with Monken, playmakers outside of TE Harold Fannin Jr . are still unknown. Concepcion could quickly climb the ranks of reliable options and prove to be one of the more explosive young players in the NFL.

 

 

 Maldonado's top Defensive Rookie of the Year candidates 
 

 1. Sonny Styles , LB, Washington Commanders (+750) 
 It's how Washington plans to use Styles that makes his case intriguing. The Commanders will want to take advantage of his ability on blitzes after Styles generated pressure on 20% of his blitz opportunities at Ohio State. He also had the lowest missed-tackle rate among linebackers in this draft class. That gives the No. 7 pick multiple ways to build a DROY résumé: tackles, sacks and impact plays.

 
 

 2. Arvell Reese , LB, New York Giants (+850) 
 As the No. 5 pick, Reese immediately steps into a starting role that will give him the snap volume needed to contend. The concern is what position those snaps will come from. With Abdul Carter and Brian Burns on the edges, Reese might be limited in the linebacker role. He can still contribute as a blitzer, but the Giants might barely blitz -- Dennard Wilson's defense in Tennessee last season ranked 28th in blitz rate. Reese's versatility would need to translate into enough splash plays to win this award.

 
 

 3. Dillon Thieneman , S, Chicago Bears (+2500) 
 As a calculated long shot, the first-round pick is already Chicago's starting strong safety. He should be around the ball plenty after playing 40% of his snaps in the box last season. Thieneman recorded 94 tackles in his final college season, while missing just 7.8% of his attempts.

 Safeties rarely win DROY, but the last one to do it was Mark Carrier with the Bears in 1990. Thieneman is worthy of bringing the award back home given his immediate role.

 
 

 4. Caleb Banks , DT, Minnesota Vikings (+7000) 
 Banks enters the season with a starting opportunity on Minnesota's defensive line, and he has the size to become an immediate interior disruptor. Although his college production was inconsistent, his pass-rush upside was considered among the best of the interior defensive linemen in his class.

 Coordinator Brian Flores can also move the No. 18 pick around his multiple-front defense to create favorable matchups. Banks' first-round pedigree and disruptive ability give him a reasonable path to win this award.

 
 

 5. Mansoor Delane , CB, Kansas City Chiefs (+1100) 
 The Chiefs traded up for the first-round cornerback to address a major need following the departures of Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson . Delane can also make impact plays as a blitzer for coordinator Steve Spagnuolo, generating pressure on 38% of his blitz opportunities in 2025 with LSU.

 Though only three cornerbacks have won DROY this century, he has the draft capital, starting role and versatility to be a strong candidate.

 

 

 Bowen's under-the-radar rookies 
 

 1. Malachi Fields , WR, New York Giants 
 Fields has the physical profile at 6-foot-4, 218 pounds to win one-on-one targets as the boundary X receiver. Plus, the third-rounder can get the ball on deep in-breakers and underneath throws. Fields is pushing for the No. 2 role in New York, and his skill set should complement that of WR1 Malik Nabers .

 

 
 

 2. Treydan Stukes , S, Las Vegas Raiders 
 The Raiders' second pick after drafting Mendoza, Stukes has seen reps with the first-team defense in camp. He has the range and instincts to play from depth in split-field or post alignments, and he brings a coverage element to new coordinator Rob Leonard's system. Look for Stukes to even align at the nickelback position.

 
 

 3. Jonah Coleman , RB, Denver Broncos 
 The Broncos landed Coleman in the fourth round, and the rookie has flashed this preseason. He has the foot quickness and vision to thrive in Denver's rushing attack, but he also adds to the pass game with his receiving skills and…

title: The story behind Steelers' viral field blessing: 'God doesn't pick sides'
summary: A missed Ravens field goal turned a routine blessing into NFL folklore. The prior of Saint Vincent Archabbey is still trying to separate faith from superstition.
full_text:
LATROBE, Pa. -- Sitting in the recliner of his monastic man cave at Saint Vincent Archabbey, the Rev. Maximilian Maxwell basked in the soft glow of his flat-screen as he soaked in the euphoria of the  Pittsburgh Steelers ' improbable Week 18 win.

 Giddy from the adrenaline rush of the  Baltimore Ravens ' missed field goal that sealed the Steelers' AFC North title and 2025 playoff berth, Father Max, the prior of the archabbey, called a few friends during the commercial break to celebrate, and as the rush simmered to a buzz, he settled back in his chair to wind down for the night.

 Then, he sat up in disbelief.

 As the broadcast resumed, Father Max watched himself on the TV walk across the gold end zone at Acrisure Stadium, sprinkling holy water, and he heard NBC play-by-play announcer Mike Tirico narrate the religious ritual.

 

 "This way," Tirico said, pointing, "is the end zone where the missed field goal happened by Tyler Loop . I want to show you what happened pregame, at 6:15 local time. This is a priest who is spreading holy water in that end zone. ... And down at that end zone is where Tyler Loop misses the field goal and allows the Steelers to win."

 Tirico's partner, Cris Collinsworth, chuckled and added, "So it's not Tyler Loop's fault."

 Tirico: "As with everything in football, it's at a higher power."

 Father Max was speechless. But his friends weren't.

 His phone started ringing, and it didn't stop ringing for days. News crews showed up at the monastery. TMZ even requested an interview. Everyone wanted to know about the priest who seemingly blessed and prayed the Steelers to the postseason and a win against their archrival.

 "I did not like the fact of having a cellphone," Father Max recently told ESPN, recalling that night. "I had received many text messages and things of that nature. And that's where it gets weird, because of the fact that people were thanking me and congratulating me."

 Anxiously waiting for the timer on his 15 minutes of fame to expire, Father Max respectfully declined all interview requests at the time. To him and the nearly 200 monks at Saint Vincent Archabbey, founded in 1846 as the first Benedictine monastery in North America, there's nothing supernatural or mystical about the blessing. The water didn't make Loop miss the field goal, and it certainly didn't determine the outcome of the game.

 "No, I don't think so," Father Max said, when asked if the Steelers won by divine intervention. "I think it was a case where something happens, that's why we play the game. That would be a case where, if all of the players competed worthily and well with virtue and went home safe and sound, that's why that blessing took place."

 

 What the cameras didn't show is that Father Max blessed the entire field before the game -- not just that one end zone. And what the mics didn't pick up was his prayer for the players' health and safety. There wasn't one word uttered urging the Steelers to win or the Ravens to lose. It's not a supernatural incantation. It's a sacred ritual, one that Father Max has performed for the past decade in tandem with the Rev. Paul Taylor.

 "It's become a nice tradition that really brings people together," said Father Paul, who is also the president of Saint Vincent College, where the Steelers held training this summer. "And we try to do it in ways that are not visible. What people want to see is the game. We're sort of the behind-the-scenes people there for the team, just people of the team. It's not about us. It's about them.

 "We pray for health and safety and freedom from injury. That's the prayer. And it's really for all the players on the field. It's not picking sides. God doesn't pick sides."

 But that didn't stop players and fans -- and certainly Ravens fans -- from speculating that the Steelers got a divinely ordained dub.

 "I was laughing with the [Pat] McAfee guys, they hit me up about that," Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers told ESPN. "They sent me the clip -- I think that's when first I saw it -- they said, 'This is why you guys won.'"

 Longtime Steelers defensive leader Cameron Heyward laughed and shook his head at the memory from Jan. 4.

 "Whenever crazy stuff happens, I'm not surprised," he said. "God's got a plan. ... God's always been a Steelers fan."

 Even second-year quarterback Will Howard , who is a practicing Catholic, admitted that his grandmother would probably say the win was divine intervention.

 "She was uber-Catholic," Howard said. "She would have been the one to be like, 'That's why you guys won. You won because the priest blessed the field.'"

 But Father Max and Father Paul are clear: Correlation doesn't imply causation. The blessings aren't the Steelers' secret weapon, and they don't dictate game outcomes. And with the initial fervor around the Week 18 blessing cooled, they now view the moment of virality as an opportunity to shine a light on the faith and the customs that come along with it.

 "It's moving away from superstition and magic and things of that nature and focusing on trying to honor that sacramental and that honest blessing," Father Max said. "That's part of the beautiful bridge between church stuff and society stuff. Someone finds this attractive, and it's up to me for them to explain it, and move it away from magic and superstition to ask for a blessing so that peace of mind and heart can reside in whatever people are asking for."

 

 Father Paul, a Western Pennsylvania native who has been at Saint Vincent since arriving as a freshman in 1983, started blessing the fields for the Steelers in 2003, but the tradition dates back to the AstroTurf at Three Rivers Stadium, Steelers team president Art Rooney II confirmed.

 "Every time we drop new turf in, we bless the field," Father Paul said. "The same here at Saint Vincent. At the beginning of every season, we bless the turf."

 As he took on more responsibilities, eventually becoming the president of Saint Vincent College in 2019, Father Paul's schedule filled up quickly. A decade ago, Father Paul wasn't available for the training camp blessing. That's when he called Father Max. Since then, the two have split blessing the field duties.

 "We, unfortunately, can't be at two places at one time," Father Max said. "So not to mix metaphors, but he goes to the bullpen for myself to help fill in for him and for the blessings."

 As part of the blessing, the priests also bury Benedictine jubilee medals inscribed with a prayer for goodness and divine presence in each corner of the new sod.

 Blessing the field is just one of the ways the priests and the Saint Vincent serves and partners with the Steelers. The college has hosted the Steelers for training camp since 1966, and the Rooney family's connection to the college and monastery dates back to Art Rooney Sr. playing prep school football games at Saint Vincent in the early 1900s and later attending Catholic retreats at the residence halls as a young adult. Some of his own children, including Art Rooney Jr., later attended the college, and now, the Steelers stay at Rooney Hall during camp.

 After the Steelers won their sixth Super Bowl in 2009, the monastery housed the trophies during training camp, and the monks helped display them for the fans.

 The archabbey also offers Mass several times a week, ones frequently attended by Steelers coach Mike McCarthy. He missed the finale of the team's annual home run derby to make a late-afternoon Saturday Mass.

 

 "It's not about, really, what we all do," said Father Paul, emphasizing the importance of hospitality in the Benedictine order. "It's about how we walk together. So having a blessing of the field or offering Mass or some sort of ministry opportunity to the organization is just really a matter of friendship. It's what we do."

 As an ambassador for the college and the archabbey, Father Paul is a frequent visitor to the sidelines of Chuck Noll Field during training camp, almost always wearing…

title: Super Bowl countdown: Ranking teams all-in on winning in 2026
summary: We stacked the top five NFL teams that need to win this season because of aging rosters, contracts or future draft capital.
full_text:
In February, ESPN will televise the  Super Bowl  for the first time. We will count down to the big game with Super Bowl-centric stories every month. 

 There are teams in the NFL that are building for the future with youth, and there are teams that are investing to win it all right now.

 Whether it is because of age, contracts or future draft capital, some teams just have a better chance to win this season's Super Bowl than they will in 2027 or 2028. From the ever-so-obvious Rams (the current Super Bowl favorites) -- who've added star power this offseason -- to teams such as the Bills and Ravens that are built around MVP-winning quarterbacks, here's a look at the five franchises that are the most "all-in" for the 2026 season.

 (As a reminder, just because a team appears to be "all-in," that doesn't mean it is guaranteed to contend; anything can happen across 17 games.)

 Note: "Average age of starters" is based on the top 12 players considering both 11 and 12 personnel on offense, as well as base and nickel personnel on defense. 

 

 

 1.  Los Angeles Rams 
 The Rams are the most obvious all-in team in the NFL this season after their blockbuster offseason moves, like trading for Myles Garrett and pulling Aaron Donald out of retirement . But it actually starts with the fact that they are rolling with a 38-year-old Matthew Stafford at quarterback. Stafford is still at the top of his game -- he just won the MVP award -- but there's a general feeling around the league that he's close to retirement , especially if the Rams manage to win Super Bowl LXI.

 

 The Rams' defense is also older, but it is loaded with star power. Donald is returning from retirement at 35, while Garrett and Poona Ford are both 31. The starters' average age of 28.1 is tied for sixth oldest in the NFL.

 Will the Rams be able to refresh their talent in next year's draft? It's going to be hard, because their first-round pick went to the Browns in the Garrett trade , while their third-round pick went to Kansas City as part of the package for cornerback Trent McDuffie . The Garrett trade also cost the Rams their second-round selection in 2028. On top of that, young stars Puka Nacua ,  Byron Young  and  Kobie Turner are playing on the final years of their rookie contracts.

 This really is a win-now situation for L.A.

 
 

 2.  Denver Broncos 
 The Broncos are older than most people realize, which is why their Super Bowl window might be closing. Denver is one of the oldest teams on both sides of the ball, but you might not notice because it has a younger quarterback in 26-year-old Bo Nix . The average age of the Broncos' projected offensive starters is 29.1, which ranks second. Left tackle  Garett Bolles  is now 34, and the whole offensive line is 28 or older. Plus, receiver  Courtland Sutton is 31 and tight end  Evan Engram is 32.

 On defense, the Broncos' average age of starters ranks fourth at 28.3. Linebackers Alex Singleton (32) and Justin Strnad (30) are both at least 30 years old, and defensive linemen  D.J. Jones (31) and Zach Allen (29) are also on the older side.

 Despite the age of this group, it is still very capable of winning. Denver made it to last season's AFC Championship Game  before suffering a 10-7 loss to the Patriots. And the Broncos recorded 68 sacks in 17 games, which left them just short of the 1984 Bears' single-season record of 72.

 With the offseason trade to acquire receiver Jaylen Waddle  and re-signing key contributors on defense, the Broncos appear to be building for another playoff run this season.

 
 

 3.  San Francisco 49ers 
 The 49ers are also a veteran team, although they've gotten younger on defense.

 Last season, San Francisco ranked third in the NFL in snap-weighted age overall. This season, the average age of their projected offensive starters is 30.3, the oldest mark in the NFL. Left tackle Trent Williams is 38. Center Jake Brendel is 34 (and his contract voids after 2026). Fullback  Kyle Juszczyk  is 35, while tight end George Kittle and wide receiver Mike Evans are both 33. Running back  Christian McCaffrey is 30.

 

 The projected starting defense averages 26.2, with linebacker Fred Warner (30) as the oldest player. San Francisco is also currently 29th in projected cap space for 2027, according to OverTheCap, although a lot of that can be solved by cutting Brandon Aiyuk and then extending Warner and Nick Bosa .

 Back in January, quarterback Brock Purdy reaffirmed his belief in the team, saying that he " 100 percent " believes the 49ers can win as soon as the 2026 season.

 
 

 4.  Buffalo Bills 
 The Bills are currently 30th in the league in 2027 cap space, and they're going to have difficulty climbing out of that hole. The only obvious candidate for a restructuring is left tackle Dion Dawkins , 32, so there will need to be cuts.

 The good news is that the Bills won't have many of their own free agents to re-sign after the 2026 season. No player who played at least 50% of snaps for the Bills last season is still on the roster with a contract that ends after this season.

 As quarterback Josh Allen , 30, approaches his ninth NFL season, the pressure is definitely on him to help Buffalo finally get over the hump. The Bills added reinforcements for him this offseason, including wide receiver  DJ Moore  and new coach Joe Brady.

 
 

 

 5.  Baltimore Ravens 
 According to OverTheCap, the Ravens have the least cap space for 2027, needing to cut $41.5 million to get under. The good news is that this can all be handled with an extension for quarterback Lamar Jackson , whose cap number for 2027 is an astonishing $84.3 million .

 But the Ravens have to actually get that deal done, and so far it just hasn't happened. Jackson represents himself without an agent, and the two sides couldn't reach a deal  this offseason. Is it possible that Jackson -- a two-time MVP -- could actually leave Baltimore? Stranger things have happened, but that is certainly not what Baltimore would want.

 Even though the Ravens missed the 2025 playoffs, they've worked this offseason to make sure that doesn't happen again. They invested heavily on defense, signing star defensive end Trey Hendrickson to a four-year, $112 million deal after a trade for  Maxx Crosby   famously fell through . 

 Is the pressure on Baltimore to make a run for the Super Bowl in 2026? Yes.

title: Panthers' Tetairoa McMillan says he's stronger, but is he more versatile, too?
summary: Now "20 pounds heavier," Carolina's second-year WR will aim to take advantage of his size over the middle.
full_text:
If Carolina Panthers wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan repeats in 2026 his production from his NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year campaign, he will join some pretty special company. Only Marques Colston, Odell Beckham Jr ., Justin Jefferson and Ja'Marr Chase have had at least 70 catches for 1,000 yards and seven touchdowns in their first two seasons.

 And though McMillan needs to stay healthy and adapt to the NFL adjusting to him after a stellar first season in Carolina, the second-year playmaker has built up his body to withstand the punishment of pro defenders and improve his strength for the season.

 McMillan says he is "almost 20 pounds heavier" since the start of his rookie season, and that additional mass should help his durability and stamina, as well as his potential versatility within the Panthers' offense, with coordinator Brad Idzik now calling the plays .

 

 "I was always a big fan, just in all the years that I played football, just being able to be versatile -- play inside, play outside -- just expand the offense in that way," McMillan said Wednesday.

 Last season, McMillan ran 515 routes, with 107 (20.7%) coming from the slot, according to NFL Next Gen Stats. When McMillan lined up wide, he had a 54.2% catch rate, but in the slot -- albeit on a much smaller sample size -- he caught the ball at a 69.7% clip. McMillan collected 18 catches for 220 yards (12.2 yards per catch) and two touchdowns inside, while posting 52 catches for 794 yards (15.3) and five touchdowns on 408 routes from the outside.

 Though McMillan's stat line looks better on the outside, the overall passing offense didn't necessarily surge in that regard, as QB passer ratings favored his limited slot targets. The passer rating for slot targets to McMillan was seven points higher (88.6 vs. 81.6) than his targets outside. Five interceptions were thrown when targeting McMillan's outside routes, but two came when he ran out of the slot.

 "He certainly played single [receiver] a lot last year as well, just giving us that big, reliable target over there," Panthers coach Dave Canales said. "But as y'all know, you can do things [on defense] into the boundary with the single-side X to help. You can cloud, you can get a safety dropping in, you can move a linebacker to kind of spy, just take a little bit of space over there.

 

 "So, there's things you can do, but as you move [the receivers] around in different spots, it gets harder and harder to try to pair up your best coverage guys, or they may have to move a corner inside, and then that creates matchups in other places."

 Canales said this week that the Panthers want to take advantage of McMillan's size over the middle. Now listed as 6-foot-5 and 220 pounds, McMillan is a big target for quarterback Bryce Young , who is 5-foot-10 and 204 pounds. So for Young, the bigger the target, the easier the completion, especially over the middle.

 "We'll use [McMillan] in a versatile way, be able to take advantage of how comfortable he is in the slot, and then also still be able to take advantage of the one-on-one opportunities when they come to us," Canales said of the Panthers' No. 8 pick in 2025 out of Arizona.

 McMillan's offseason weight gain was prompted by what he lost during his rookie campaign. Listed at 212 pounds last season, the wide receiver said this spring that he got lighter as the season progressed, affecting his physicality.

 

 "In college, whenever I was heavier, I was stronger, faster, and that's how I feel right now," McMillan said. "Last year ... I didn't feel like myself, like I wasn't moving as good, didn't feel as powerful. Now, I feel like I got a lot [of strength] back."

 Canales said McMillan was "a man on a mission to get stronger" this offseason. The coach also said the additional mass should help the receiver's effectiveness against press coverage on the outside. It'll also help when McMillan runs into traffic out of the slot.

 With Jalen Coker healthy to begin the season, the Panthers can rotate their receivers around the formation. McMillan, Coker, Xavier Legette and Brycen Tremayne all can move around, and slot players such as Jimmy Horn Jr . and John Metchie III can add wrinkles to various packages.

 But this Panthers offense is built around McMillan. And his fluidity is essential for creating mismatches in Idzik's playbook.

 "[The slot] allows me to play decoy sometimes; it allows me to get open," McMillan said. "It allows everybody, just the offense, to flow easily."

title: Chase Brown won't be overlooked in Bengals' offense
summary: The Bengals plan to reduce dramatically their shotgun snaps in hopes of using Brown more all over the field.
full_text:
CINCINNATI -- For all the money the  Cincinnati Bengals  have spent on quarterback Joe Burrow and the passing attack, it can be easy to overlook running back Chase Brown .

 But Burrow can't be lumped into that group. At the beginning of training camp, Burrow offered a glimpse into how Brown's usage might look in Cincinnati's revamped 2026 offense. Throughout training camp, Cincinnati has looked at tweaking its scheme, featuring more reps with Burrow lined up under center.

 No matter how it's sliced, expect Brown to play a major role in how the Bengals operate.

 "Obviously we're going to get the ball in (wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase )'s hands as many times as we can," Burrow said in late July. "But I think a close second is Chase Brown just because of how explosive he is and the things he can do with the ball in his hands."

 Last season, Brown was ninth among all running backs with 1,456 scrimmage yards. Of that total, Brown ranked sixth in his position with 437 receiving yards.

 Starting in 2024, Brown has been the team's featured running back. And over time, he has settled into the position and been a featured player in a high-powered offense that features Burrow, Chase and wide receiver Tee Higgins .

 Burrow praised Brown's versatility in not just what he did with the ball but also how he helps the offense in pass protection.

 "I think there's very few backs in this league that you can say that about," Burrow said. "And when you have a guy like that, you don't have to take him off the field.

 "You can put him in on so many different packages. You can build different packages for him in different places on the field."

 That versatility is also a testament to his growth as well. Bengals assistant Justin Hill, who is in his sixth season coaching the team's running backs, said Brown has steadily improved each year since the Bengals took him in the fifth round of the 2023 draft.

 The more experienced and skilled he has become, the more Cincinnati has tried to manufacture ways to take advantage of Brown's skillset.

 "We're going to try to find ways to just move him around and showcase what he can do," Hill told ESPN in August. "Not only in the backfield, under center, in the gun, but also (receiving out of the backfield) as well."

 Just how much the Bengals' offense will change with going under center has been a major topic of conversation. Cincinnati has been one of the most shotgun-heavy teams in recent years. Last season, the Bengals ranked second in that category at 81.4%, per ESPN Research.

 But that dwindled over the year as the Bengals tried to find more balance, even after Burrow returned for the final six games following a turf toe injury. That pursuit extended into this offseason.

 And after a full training camp and preseason, that experimentation has proven to be successful. Earlier this week, Bengals coach Zac Taylor said he feels good about where the team is at schematically and likes the inventory available to him as a playcaller.

 Cincinnati will still lean on the things that have been successful over the years. But going under center with Brown and the running backs carrying the workload could be a valuable wrinkle at various points this season.

 "You're going to have situations throughout the season where you're going to be in some cold weather games or maybe just things aren't clicking in the pass game," said Bengals assistant James Casey, the team's run game coordinator. "You have got to be able to run the ball to win some games and close some games out."

 That style of offense is also more conducive to explosive rushing plays, which is something the Bengals have lacked over the years. And that's another area where Brown can be effective.

 "If he can get that little crease, he's got the speed and he's strong enough to be able to get through it," Casey said. "And he's not timid. He's going to be able to hit it."

 This season is shaping up to be a big year for Brown. He's entering the final year of his rookie contract after the offseason failed to materialize an extension. Brown is among many Bengals who are looking to cash in on their second NFL contracts.

 But on the cusp of the season, Brown felt good about where things stand both for himself and the team.

 "This is one of the best training camps I've been a part of, not only for myself but as a team," Brown said. "Just seeing the way that everybody is operating, it's really encouraging.

 "I'm excited about what we're going to do this year and I feel like we're capable of a lot."

title: Touring the Denver Broncos' new $175 million team facility
summary: The 240,000 square-foot facility opened this summer and is the jewel of the Broncos' quest for a championship. Let's peek inside.
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- There's a small hill on Broncos Parkway that crests in front of the Arapahoe County Sheriff's Department. With the Rocky Mountains in the rearview mirror, drivers spent decades seeing a blue building on the corner as they came down the backslide of the slope and rolled up to the stoplight. When peeking through the glass doors of that building, one could see the Denver Broncos ' Super Bowl trophies.

 But after more than two years of digging, pounding and the use of a nine-story crane, the Broncos believe they can see the future from that hill. Their gleaming new complex, which cost $175 million according to the team, casts a significant late-afternoon shadow over the old place.

 "I said it last year when they were still building it, I say 'look at it, just look at it,'" running back J.K. Dobbins said. "How are you going to be a player and you see the coaches, the team, the people and where we go every day and not want to be here? Nobody else has one of these."

 

 It was one of the first priorities of the Walton-Penner ownership group, a project to get almost all the team's employees under one roof, make the football operation more efficient day-to-day and make the Broncos a destination franchise to attract the best players and coaches.

 "Ten out of 10, it's a wellness center," defensive tackle D.J. Jones said. "I think we just needed a new locker room, but we went in the grocery store and got more than milk. So, I love it."

 Let's take a tour of the Broncos' new digs:

 
 IT MIGHT BE easier to list things that aren't in the new building. It's 240,000 square feet -- roughly 5.5 acres spread over three floors of state-of-the-art workplace -- that had Broncos owner/CEO Greg Penner answering questions about whether the new headquarters was too comfortable to produce a championship team.

 "Well, I think you've met our head coach [Sean Payton]," Penner said with wry smile. "So, I'm not worried about them not working hard enough. ... We're trying to raise the expectations, and our expectation is we want to win championships, and we're going to do everything it takes and provide the resources that are necessary to do it."

 The new building is 30% larger than the team's former home, and the Broncos say the "peak daily workforce" is 450 people, including players and coaches.

 

 The entire project took a total 750,000 man hours over 22 months. The black spruce timbers, a prominent feature on the exterior of the building as well as inside on the top floor, are from Chibougamau, Quebec.

 "Every day I walk the building, I see different parts for the first time post-construction and I think it's amazing," Broncos president Damani Leech said. "It's a testament to ownership, to Greg and Carrie, the investment they've made into football ... but also our business to ... create culture, to design a building with football in mind.

 "I love coming to work every day, and I think everybody else does, too."

 

 
 GREG AND CARRIE Penner have made the phrase "player path" a foundational premise of the facility. In the Broncos' former complex, players, coaches and staff had to leave the main building and cross a parking lot to get to the weight room. They also had to walk across two practice fields to get to their indoor practice building.

 That's all well and good when it's sunny and warm, but it's a completely different proposition when the snow comes roaring down from the mountains.

 "You would go outside to go back inside," offensive tackle Mike McGlinchey said.

 

 The first floor of the building is the players' primary place. They have a parking garage, locker room, equipment room, training room, weight room, cafeteria and the hallway to the indoor practice facility. And they are all close to each other. There is even a lap pool for players like safety Brandon Jones , who used to make early morning stops at a local rec center to swim, to get in their laps.

 

 It's much bigger and better equipped than the old complex. The training room alone, where the medical and training staff operate, includes a cryotherapy room, dry float tank, ammortal chamber (a NASA-inspired zero gravity bed to help muscle recovery as well as stress reduction), hyperbaric chamber, sauna, therapy pools and sleep pods.

 "It's a great office for the players to get to come to every day," Leech said. "[The locker room] is a really special place with a centralized sort of living room area for them to gather and spend time."

 The locker room is five times larger than the old locker room and has 102 lockers, so it can easily accommodate the players when the roster is at 90 or 91 players in training camp or at 53 in regular season, in addition to the practice squad and players on injured reserve.

 

 
 LET'S MOVE UP to the second floor and the football nerve center. Payton, general manager George Paton and Penner have the keystone offices. But the coaching, personnel and scouting staffs are there, too, with plenty of meeting space for the offensive and defensive coaches. The IT staff, video staff and operations staff are also on this floor.

 It has a room specially dedicated to the team's draft preparations and use during draft weekend. In the old complex, Paton, Payton, coaches and the scouting staff would be in the generic team meeting room during draft season.

 

 "Everything is state-of-the-art," cornerback Pat Surtain II said. "When I first got in ... I was looking at it and I was like, 'Wow.' I was in awe."

 According to Penner, "everything is connected," with hallways designed and built to make the daily flow between every department on the floor as efficient as possible. One quirk in the old building was there was no way for people to walk the length of the first floor without going through the locker room, so employees from other departments would go up a flight of stairs to cross above the locker room and back down a flight of stairs to complete the journey.

 The space for the Broncos' football operations is now 100,000 square feet, nearly half the total square footage of the building.

 
 BEYOND THE BELLS and whistles, the biggest functional change can be seen on the third floor. The open space that surrounds Carrie Penner's and Leech's offices now includes 85 employees who were previously located at the stadium. There are 12 different business departments on the floor. There is also an employee fitness center and a golf simulator -- "I've seen players up there," Greg Penner said.

 Nods to the franchise's history are all over the building but are especially evident on this floor. Along with memorabilia on the walls, the conference rooms have been given names like Miles (the mascot), Thunder (the horse that runs the field after touchdowns) and Barrel Man (a Broncos superfan).

 

 The windows offer an uninhibited view of the mountains to the west. There is also a rooftop patio, which was used for players' families during training camp and will be utilized for events throughout the season.

 "What I think is unique about this building is that it is distinctly Colorado," Leech said. "I think people walk the building and they feel like they understand that this is the Denver Broncos' training facility.

 "I love the third floor ... the elevated ceilings, the mass timber is a great place for me to come and work every day. I was begging for the golf simulator and I got it, so there's really nothing that we didn't get. Nothing."

 The Broncos' former facility is set to be demolished during the season. In its place will be a berm that will provide the viewing area for fans for future training camps.
