title: Colts' Daniel Jones has one box left to check in dramatic return
summary: When the quarterback faces the Ravens in Week 1, it will be yet another attempt to rise from disappointment.
full_text:
INDIANAPOLIS --  Daniel Jones is not paid to play slow-pitch softball. But, competitor that he is, the Indianapolis Colts quarterback was going to give it a go during his first at-bat in a recent charity softball game that featured the Colts and  Indiana Pacers .

 With Pacers star Tyrese Haliburton on the mound at Victory Field in downtown Indianapolis, Jones took his best swing and made solid contact. The ball soared, and Jones paused for a moment to admire its flight.

 Once the ball cleared the short, makeshift fence in right field for a home run, the crowd cheered as Jones rounded the bases. The thousands attending seemed to embrace the opportunity to celebrate Jones. They likely hope there soon will be further opportunities to do the same down the street at Lucas Oil Stadium.

 "I realized pretty quickly when I got here last year just how supportive these fans are," Jones said.

 It was a much different reception than anything Jones witnessed during his final season playing in New York, when he was once jeered and booed by Giants fans while walking to his car at MetLife Stadium after one of his final games there in 2024.

 It would have been difficult back then to envision the embattled Jones headlining an event alongside a beloved star such as Haliburton. Jones' NFL career would soon hit rock bottom when he was benched and, later, released by the Giants, winding up stashed on the  Minnesota Vikings ' practice squad.

 "That was definitely a low point," he said.

 Now, two contracts and one torn Achilles later, Jones is exactly where he wants to be. And if he can meet expectations this season -- bounce back from the torn right Achilles and reignite the Colts' offense as he did last season before his injury -- Jones thinks he might have found a long-term home.

 

 "That's always the goal," Jones said, "to be somewhere long term and build something."

 Jones has reversed his fortunes before, and the Colts are betting he can do it again. He bounced back after his tumultuous tenure in New York, reaching a point where now his likeness adorns the side of a 33-story luxury hotel in downtown Indianapolis. Finishing 2025 with, easily, the best season of his career did wonders for rehabilitating his reputation.

 "I'm really excited to see how everything pans out for him," said Haliburton, who has developed a bit of a kinship with Jones as Haliburton rebounds from his own Achilles tear. "I know he's going to do great, and I'm really excited that he's back. And I know the city is, as well."

 But can Jones do it again and put together another impressive season after his injury? Everything that has happened in recent months suggests the answer could be yes. Jones commanded the first-team offense during training camp, missing no days of practice, and he remains on track to play against the Baltimore Ravens in the Colts' opener Sept. 13 ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ). His comeback has been stunning even to those who've seen it up close.

 "It was super hard to envision it because it's an Achilles," tight end Mo Alie-Cox said. "... There weren't many great examples of somebody coming back that fast. And then we came back for OTAs, he's already throwing, running. Then, he starts taking parts and 7-on-7, and I'm like, 'Hold on, this might be real.'"

 It has all the makings of a great story. As Jones starts to reflect on what has transpired the past two years, the details he offers make that clearer.

 He thought back to his final weeks in New York and admitted he could see where things were headed. His last start was an overtime loss to the Carolina Panthers in Week 10 of the 2024 season. He threw two interceptions, and the Giants fell to 2-8 in a game played in Germany. The back page of the New York Post the following morning declared, in large font, "THE WURST!"

 "I wasn't playing well, and things weren't going our way," Jones said. "I remember the game in Germany was tough, and then, in the bye week, you kind of got an idea of what might happen."

 Jones was benched before the Giants' next game, with Tommy DeVito ascending to the starting role. The Giants were reluctant to use Jones even in practice, given the likelihood they would cut him following the season. That meant ensuring they weren't on the hook for paying the $23 million injury guarantee they'd owe if he got hurt.

 

 "I couldn't practice, I couldn't work out, I couldn't really do anything," Jones said. "So, I was just kind of there."

 Jones appealed to ownership to release him. The request was granted, and Jones was without a team for the first time. He was the Giants' first-round pick in 2019 and had shown enough to be rewarded with a four-year, $160 million contract. But just like that, his time there was over.

 "You're not expecting to be dealing with all that and looking for a new place to go at that point in the season," Jones said.

 Jones is measured and extremely private. But those who know him confirm the end of his New York experience was difficult on him. The turmoil there played a role in the Colts' decision to spend more on Jones' recent two-year, $88 million extension, according to a source, hoping it would signal what Indianapolis views as a true commitment.

 Jones finished the season with the Vikings, hoping to learn from their coach Kevin O'Connell, who is considered a quarterback specialist. Then, in free agency during spring 2025, the Colts offered an appealing situation: compete with Anthony Richardson Sr . for the starting job in Indy. The Colts had promised to add quarterback competition, but the choice of Jones on a one-year $14 million contract produced laughs in some corners.

 By the fall, no one was laughing.

 Jones started fast, winning the job and joining forces with coach Shane Steichen to torch defenses. The Colts had the best record in the NFL by Week 10 (8-2), and Jones was sizzling. Last season, he ranked top 10 among quarterbacks in completion rate (68%), QBR (63.0) and yards per attempt (8.1).

 But Jones couldn't finish the job. He tore his right Achilles at Jacksonville in December. Jones immediately knew it, slamming his helmet into the turf in despair.

 "I felt like someone kicked me really hard in the back of the leg, and I looked around and there was nobody there," Jones said. "And then you get up and your ankle's just kind of loose. At that point, I knew."

 He continued, "At first, you're just in disbelief. You're like, 'No way this is happening right now. Not now.'

 "There's just disappointment. I think the season to that point was the most fun I had playing football in the NFL. We had played well... I think you realize pretty quickly you're not going to be a part of that anymore. And that was the toughest part."

 The Colts lost their next four games and missed the playoffs, with former Colts quarterback Philip Rivers coming out of retirement in an unsuccessful bid to save the season.

 But even as the Colts tried to pick up the pieces from another lost campaign -- they haven't made the playoffs since 2020 -- they immediately turned their attention to running it back with Jones. Steichen and GM Chris Ballard believed they had seen enough to bank on him. Owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon quickly concurred.

 Jones was re-signed in March, even before his rehab had progressed to the point of throwing again. But as offseason workouts intensified, Jones became more and more involved. He studied the details of how quarterbacks such as  Aaron Rodgers and Kirk Cousins had come back from their Achilles injuries. He worked unceasingly in his rehab. And it was all paying off.

 When training camp began, the Colts removed the restrictions.

 "The doctors," according to Steichen, "said, 'Hey, let's let him go.'"

 Jones has practiced every day since the start of training camp and taken practically every first-team snap. It was a departure from last year's camp, when he and Richardson were competing and splitting reps.

 "He had almost 450 more throws than he did a year…

title: Young Miami Dolphins embracing underdog mentality in 2026
summary: Miami, with the youngest roster in the NFL, is turning preseason pessimism into fuel for 2026.
full_text:
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. -- The Miami Dolphins are an underdog in all 17 of their games this season, according to ESPN's matchup predictor. They say they are not paying attention to any predictions, but are embracing the underdog mentality the low expectations have helped create.

 The Dolphins' projected win total for the 2026 season is 4.5 games, and early mock drafts already have them earning the No. 1 pick in the 2027 draft.

 

 First-year coach Jeff Hafley said there will be an increased focus on player development this season, but the goal is still to win games. Whether anyone else believes they're capable of doing so is none of Miami's concern.

 "I don't think we have a choice [but to have an underdog mindset], honestly," linebacker Jordyn Brooks said. "I don't think there's one outlet on social media, anybody that's got us picked to win anything. Not that it matters, but that's just what it is. I don't think any of our opponents respect us. So, 100% underdog mindset, and I think that's always the best position to be in.

 "We're going to carry that mindset into the season and have that 'us against the world' mentality and do our best to win football games."

 Miami will field the youngest roster in the NFL this season, thanks in part to a 13-player rookie class -- all of whom made the initial 53-man roster, although seventh-round pick Max Llewellyn was waived and re-signed to the practice squad.

 This was always the plan for the Dolphins, who will absorb an NFL-record $180 million of dead cap money in an effort to get younger and cheaper. That youth might not help the team win games right away, but Hafley said it will help build a foundation for the future.

 "We knew we'd be a young team," he said. "And that's all along, we've talked about developing and I've talked about the process and I've talked about the foundation and I've talked about the culture. Usually, you start those things and you're pretty young. I mean, you can look at that and say, 'Oh, we're so young.' I look at that and I'm excited about that. We are excited to develop that. We're excited for the hunger that they have.

 

 "You mix in some good vets in the pieces that I've said all along that we already have here, and I'm excited to get the process started. And again, that's with the intent to win games, right? I think everybody has misconstrued that with the end result, winning, but it's going to be fun to get these guys going."

 One of Miami's 13 draft picks, second-round linebacker Jacob Rodriguez , progressed to a point this summer where the team felt comfortable making one of its surprise moves of the offseason -- cutting last year's starter, Tyrel Dodson .

 Brooks called Rodriguez a "rookie vet" who has gotten "better and better" since OTAs. And Hafley said he's excited about where the former Texas Tech star is on the eve of his rookie season. Rodriguez said Miami's rookie class is tight-knit and ready to accept the responsibility of rebuilding a team that has turned in consecutive losing seasons for the first time since 2019.

 

 "I think coming from college, we're all fresh. We all want to do the right thing," he said. "We're all close, we want to come together and try to play the best football we can. There's a lot of responsibility to that, but I think I just kind of mentioned it: You got a job to do. You got to be a pro about it and you got to come in and do the right thing.

 "If you love football and don't love as much of what football can do for you and you're in here all the time, you're having fun, you're enjoying the people around you, I think you can start having fun with this and start playing well."

 The Dolphins start the season next week with a two-game road trip against the Las Vegas Raiders and San Francisco 49ers . Then they host the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 3 to round out the opening month. According to Mike Clay's season projections , their highest probability to win a game will come in their Week 12 home matchup with the New York Jets  (33%).

 Not that it matters to anyone in Miami's locker room.

 "I don't pay attention to that stuff, I never have," defensive tackle Zach Sieler said. "I'm kind of an underdog story my whole life, my whole career. So, I really don't. The outside noise and all that stuff. There hasn't been a single snap of football played yet this year. So to do that, it's all off of last season's whatever. We've all seen guys and teams make massive jumps in a matter of a year.

 "I'm very excited for this team and where we're going to go, and I think guys have the passion, the love and the 'know-how' to want to be the best, every day."

title: Will Kyler Murray end the Vikings' tragicomic QB history?
summary: Despite names you know -- Moon, Culpepper, Favre, Cousins -- Minnesota hasn't had a franchise QB since Tarkenton.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- Long before he signed with the Minnesota Vikings this spring, Kyler Murray understood the tragicomic nature of their attempt to find a stable long-term quarterback. 

 Murray grew up in Texas but has been a Vikings fan since playing for a youth football team by the same name, and he remembers watching quarterback Brett Favre -- the 40-year-old future Hall of Famer in his first year with the Vikings -- throw an interception late in the fourth quarter of the 2009 NFC Championship Game. 

 "I cried real tears that day," Murray said. 

 He'll step on the U.S. Bank Stadium field Sept. 13 against the Green Bay Packers ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ) as the Vikings' fourth different Week 1 starter in four years. That only begins to describe the team's itinerant -- but often successful -- quarterback turnstile. 

 Barring injury or an unexpected level of ineffectiveness, Murray will finish this season as the 18th different quarterback to lead the Vikings in passing since the NFL's free agency era began in 1993. The only teams with more are the Cleveland Browns (20) and Washington Commanders (19), according to ESPN Research. 

 

 Generations of Vikings team builders have tried everything. 

 They've used four first-round draft picks to select quarterbacks, but three of them -- Daunte Culpepper , Teddy Bridgewater and J.J. McCarthy -- had their careers derailed by injuries before they turned 28. The fourth, Christian Ponder , was benched at age 25. 

 They've acquired two future Hall of Fame passers, Favre and Warren Moon , and tried to lure a third out of retirement ( Dan Marino ). Some of the team's leadership wanted to sign another future Hall of Famer, Aaron Rodgers , in 2025. 

 They've tapped veteran backups from Gus Frerotte to Matt Cassel to Case Keenum to Sam Darnold , and acquired three players drafted with the No. 1 pick ( Jeff George , Sam Bradford and Murray). 

 "And probably the one that had the longest tenure and best career there was Kirk Cousins ," said Brad Johnson , who had two stints as the starter in Minnesota from 1996 to 1998 and 2005 to 2006.

 

 The Vikings lured Cousins in free agency with a fully guaranteed contract and ultimately paid him $185 million -- more than any player in their history -- to lead them in passing from 2018 to 2023. That stint was the longest of any Vikings quarterback since Tommy Kramer, whose final season as a full-time starter was 1986. 

 At the same time, however, Minnesota has provided a platform for some of the NFL's best collective quarterback play in the free agent era. From 1993 to 2025, Vikings quarterbacks have the league's sixth-best passer rating (88.5). 

 In 1994 and 1995, Moon doubled his career total of seasons with at least 4,000 passing yards. Randall Cunningham was an All-Pro in 1998 and finished second in MVP voting. Cunningham, George (1999), Culpepper (2004), Favre (2009), Bradford (2016), Keenum (2017), Cousins (2019) and Darnold (2024) all produced the best passer rating of their careers while playing in Minnesota.

 As Murray looks for a career reset of his own after seven seasons with the Arizona Cardinals , he'll benefit from what Hall of Fame receiver Cris Carter calls the "magic" that happens when a quarterback joins the Vikings. 

 "When you come in here, regardless of what you've done or what people said in [previous] fanbases and everything, we're going to support you," Carter said. "We're going to put some dudes around and behind you. Dudes have career years and then their careers change. And I'm a witness to that. I know it's real."

 

 

 The '90s, free agency and draft woes 
 Jeff Diamond remembers the motto 50 years later. After joining the Vikings as a public relations official in 1976, he heard general manager Mike Lynn repeat one team-building philosophy more than any other. 

 "The most important player on the team is the starting quarterback," Lynn would say, according to Diamond. "The second most important player is the No. 2 quarterback."

 It was a nod to both the past and future of the franchise. 

 Diamond rose to vice president in 1990 and served as the Vikings' de facto general manager. By then, he had seen two backup quarterbacks lead the Vikings to the NFC Championship Game: Bob Lee in 1977 and Wade Wilson in 1987. It would later happen two more times: with Cunningham in 1998 and Keenum in 2017.

 In 1992, Diamond and Dennis Green, Minnesota's head coach from 1992 to 2001, felt so strongly about building quarterback depth that they kept Johnson -- a ninth-round pick in that year's draft -- as a fourth quarterback on what was then a 47-man roster. 

 In 1993, however, NFL teams got a new tool for team-building: unrestricted free agency. The Vikings dipped in right away, signing longtime Bears starter Jim McMahon to replace incumbent Rich Gannon , whom they traded to Washington.

 

 McMahon gave way to Moon in 1994. Johnson took over in 1996, and Cunningham stepped in early during the 1998 season when Johnson fractured a bone in his right leg. The revolving door of those years did not surprise Gannon, who would eventually develop into an MVP with the Oakland Raiders , whom he led to Super Bowl XXXVII. Green never developed personal relationships with his quarterbacks, Gannon said, and that made it easier for the coach to move from one to another almost each year.

 "I thought he was a good football coach," Gannon said of Green, who died in 2016. "He was good at assembling a staff and was really good at managing that stuff. He was a horrible communicator. He did not realize the important nature of that relationship between head coach and quarterback."

 The constant turnover was in part a byproduct of draft decisions. After drafting Kramer at No. 27 in 1977, the Vikings didn't use a pick higher than Round 4 to draft a quarterback until selecting Culpepper in 1999.

 Consistent playoff success had lowered their position in the first round, and the 1989 trade for Herschel Walker that sent,  among other assets , three first-round and three second-round picks to the Cowboys gutted their next three drafts.

 So when Diamond traded Johnson to Washington after the 1998 season, securing a package of draft picks that included the No. 11 spot in 1998, a fierce debate broke out in the Vikings' draft room.

 Should they attempt to slow the turnstile and dip into a well-regarded quarterback class? Or should they use the No. 11 pick on edge rusher Jevon Kearse , who would elevate a defense to match the explosive offense of their 15-1 team from the previous season?

 "Kearse would really be more impactful in that '99 season with a team that was Super Bowl-quality," Diamond said. "So it was very difficult to make that pivot to Culpepper, but for the future of the franchise, it was probably the right move at the time."

 Kearse went five spots later to the Tennessee Titans . He earned All-Pro honors as a rookie with 14.5 sacks in helping the Titans advance to Super Bowl XXXIV. Culpepper did not play as a rookie, as George took over for Cunningham. But Culpepper started for parts of six seasons from 2000 to 2005, until he tore three ligaments in his right knee early in 2005 at age 28. 

 "If Culpepper had not had that terrible knee injury, it would've been a great pick," said Diamond, who departed the Vikings shortly after the 1999 draft to join, ironically, the Titans as team president. "And it was still a good enough pick because they got several good years out of him. It was just one of so many strange, difficult situations."

 
 

 Hall of Fame receivers and offensive-minded coaches 

 Culpepper had a strong arm and, at 265 pounds, was difficult to tackle. He also benefited from having two future Hall of Fame receivers in his first two seasons as the Vikings' starter (Carter and Randy Moss ) and at least one in five of his six. 

 In fact, Vikings quarterbacks since 1993 have had at least one Hall of Fame receiver -- or, in the case of Justin Jefferson , one who…

title: What will Patriots do if RB TreVeyon Henderson is out Week 1?
summary: Henderson did not practice on Saturday, raising some questions about New England's lack of proven depth at running back.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Henderson's status: Running back TreVeyon Henderson played in every regular-season and playoff game during his rookie season in 2025, giving the Patriots a speedy option who was a threat to score on any one play.

 So the uncertainty regarding his status for Wednesday's season opener at the Seattle Seahawks (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC) -- due to an ankle injury that has kept him out of practice since Aug. 24 -- is the type of adversity he hasn't been accustomed to in the NFL. It also sparks a question: If Henderson doesn't play or is limited in what he can do, how do the Patriots handle the running back repetitions?

 Rhamondre Stevenson would have been the clear-cut starter regardless, just as he was last season when he played 46 snaps in the opener to Henderson's 25. Stevenson said he came out of training camp feeling great physically. His knack for blitz pickup has earned him the highest degree of confidence from the coaching staff, with coach Mike Vrabel saying Saturday that "the way he finished last year was exciting."

 "I love the way that Rhamondre protects," Vrabel said early in training camp. "If you have backs that can pick up pressure, it's one thing to be able to get over there and know where the pressure is coming from. It's another [thing] to go block them."

 The only other running back on the 53-man roster is first-year player Corey Kiner , whom the Patriots acquired in a trade from the Arizona Cardinals on Aug. 28 to fill the void created when Terrell Jennings was placed on injured reserve Aug. 13. Vrabel mentioned the Patriots had attempted to sign Kiner ("a good young runner") after the 2025 draft when he instead went to the 49ers. Kiner (5-foot-9, 209 pounds) has four games and 30 offensive snaps of NFL experience, so thrusting him into an expanded role in a frenzied Seattle environment just 13 days after he joined the Patriots would be asking a lot.

 

 That's why Lan Larison (5-11, 209) and/or Hassan Haskins (6-2, 228) have a strong chance to be elevated from the practice squad. Larison, a second-year player from UC Davis, spent last season on injured reserve (foot) after initially signing with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent. Haskins is a four-year veteran who broke into the NFL on Vrabel's Tennessee Titans squad in 2023.

 Larison gets the edge in terms of background in coordinator Josh McDaniels' system (critical with pass protection in mind), while Haskins would be the pick if NFL experience (44 games) was deemed a priority. Both factor into the mix on special teams, especially on punt protection, which is an area the Patriots have spent countless hours practicing throughout the summer.

 "Guys have different strengths. There's a little bit of everything, and we'll see who we end up using for the game," Vrabel said.

 Henderson totaled 911 yards on 180 carries (5.1 average) in the 2025 regular season, with nine touchdowns. He became the first player in team history to have four 50-yard runs or rushing touchdowns in a single season, while adding nine receptions for 35 yards and one touchdown.

 The Patriots focused on their first- and second-down game plan in Thursday's practice without him. And then on Saturday, they worked with full shoulder pads and blocked and hit, according to QB Drake Maye .

 A Stevenson-Henderson one-two punch, with the addition of veteran free agent fullback Reggie Gilliam , had the Patriots feeling good about the potential of the running game throughout training camp. Then Henderson injured his ankle, clouding the outlook for the NFL's opener. 

 2. Thin at OLB: Arguably the biggest surprise heading into the season is how light the roster and practice squad look at outside linebacker, especially with Vrabel saying it wasn't a surprise to him that veteran Harold Landry III is starting the season on the physically unable to perform list -- meaning Landry will miss a minimum of four games.

 Dre'Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder are the starters, with rookies Gabe Jacas (second round) and Quintayvious Hutchins (seventh round) the top backups and Jose Ramirez (four career games played with Buccaneers in 2024) on the practice squad. Asked what he likes about the group on sports radio WEEI, Vrabel noted Jones' veteran presence, Ponder's consistency and then "daily improvement" from Jacas and Hutchins.

 The possibility that Jacas and Hutchins are one snap away from a front-line defensive role is a reminder of how important it will be for the Patriots to avoid injuries, which was a key to their 2025 success.

 3. A.J mentors Jacas: Receiver A.J. Brown remembers how hard Vrabel was on him as a rookie with the Titans in 2019, and he sees some similarities to how rookie Jacas is being coached by Vrabel this year. So, Brown recently approached Jacas to have a chat.

 

 "Vrabel is on him -- really tough. I'll be sitting in my chair laughing, just to see the process and witness it all over again," Brown said. "I don't have any worries for Gabe; he's been locked in. Hopefully my words help."

 4. 'We are firemen': The latest episode of the Patriots-produced "Forged in Foxborough" was released late last week, with the behind-the-scenes look into team meetings and Vrabel's messaging among the notable highlights. Vrabel showed the team boxing trainer Teddy Atlas' "We are firemen" corner speech to amplify the identity he hopes to create. There were also clips of Vrabel calling out Brown and defensive tackle Milton Williams , showing that he holds some of the team's best players accountable in front of everyone.

 The Atlas speech hit home with defensive tackle Leonard Taylor III .

 "It's about staying laser focused to put out the fire," he said. "It's going into this week with a mindset that we need everybody -- you can't put out the fire with just one person."

 5. Gonzo looms: When it comes to cornerback Christian Gonzalez and the Patriots negotiating a contract extension, Vrabel said Saturday that he doesn't get involved in negotiations but takes an active role "in trying to get the situation resolved." He referred to it as a "delicate balance."

 Gonzalez said Saturday that he didn't have anything to share on where negotiations stand, and Vrabel -- who expressed how he wants to coach Gonzalez -- didn't budge when asked if he felt a resolution was close.

 "I think whenever the deal is done, that's when it'll be resolved. I don't have a timetable," Vrabel said.

 6. Crownover's kudos: On the upcoming episode of the "Patriots All Access" show that airs Tuesday on the team website, Vrabel said he showed one play from a 37-13 loss in the preseason finale to the team. It was rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover 's effort following an interception when he sprinted to take out one Browns player before making the tackle. Vrabel noted it came with the team trailing with four minutes left, and that Crownover's play was the type to earn instant respect from veterans.

 

 A sixth-round pick from Texas A&M who is No. 4 on the offensive tackle depth chart, Crownover was pumped to be recognized in front of his peers.

 "We're trying to set a point for our effort and finish -- knowing you're never giving up on a play. In the meeting room, when you get called out by the head coach for that, it's a good feeling," he said. 

 7. Waiver claims : The Patriots were 31st in the waiver claim order after cut-down day, so it was reasonable to expect they would miss out on some of their targets. Turns out they didn't.

 League sources said the Patriots were the only team to put in a claim on the following five players: edge rusher  Jamal Hill (Texans), tight end Cameron Latu (Eagles) and linebackers Shaka Heyward (Bengals), Erick Hunter (Lions) and Darius Muasau (Giants). They were awarded Muasau and Latu, and pulled back their claims on Heyward, Hunter and Hill. They signed Hunter a few days later.

title: Does OBJ still got it? Fans and teammates seem to think so
summary: The WR is back with New York after eight years. Fans and teammates are all in on OBJ's New York revival.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- In August, the New York Giants trickled out for a training camp practice at The Greenbrier in White Sulphur Springs, West Virginia. Popular running back Cam Skattebo came out early. He riled up 1,500 or so fans that day with his trademark 'Wooooooo!' upon arrival. Those in the stands or lined up against the fence ate it up.

 Jaxson Dart and the quarterbacks came later. Fans of all ages perked up with excitement, letting out a loud cheer for the player they anticipate will become the face of the franchise.

 It would have been the loudest ovation for any player -- had Odell Beckham Jr . not returned to the Giants this offseason. Somewhere in between Dart and Skattebo making their way onto the field, Beckham, one of the former faces of the franchise, inconspicuously began warming up and stretching. When the fans realized, they went nuts.

 Such a scene repeated itself on a daily basis -- Beckham was undoubtedly the most popular player at training camp. The Giants are a forgiving fanbase after Beckham left on a sour note after the 2018 season -- his behavior and distractions reached a point where then-general manager Dave Gettleman wanted him off the roster and traded him to the Cleveland Browns .

 Beckham, 33, is back eight years later and it's as if none of that ever happened. He has being embraced by a fanbase that hasn't seen much exciting football since his departure -- only one winning season in seven years. They're hoping the former Pro Bowler can look like some semblance of the receiver who started his career with three straight seasons of at least 90 receptions and 1,300 yards.

 "What I love about Odell is he's unapologetically himself," said Olivia Schmidt, a 30-year-old diehard fan and season-ticket holder. "The New York attitude is almost engrained in him and something about him keeps you engaged. I think I'm drawn to that combination of confidence, edge, personality, and talent. He has a presence that you can feel, and quite frankly the Giants have been missing that since he's been gone. When he's playing, you can't help but watch."

 West Virginia was just a microcosm of the love affair. The No. 1 question asked to Giants reporters this summer was, by a wide margin: "Is Odell going to make the roster?"

 

 Ultimately, he did, earning his way onto the 53-man roster with a strong summer after a year out of the league. The most popular Giant of the last decade is back, with his presence and reputation hovering over the team.

 "When I first got here, I feel like [Odell] was almost like a unicorn, like a mythical creature that departed right before I got here," said veteran receiver Darius Slayton , who was drafted a month after Beckham was traded. "And it was like there was murmurs and whispers and legends and I never saw any of it. And then here I am on the back end being able to play with him on his return. So it's definitely cool for sure."

 Most of Beckham's teammates were in middle or elementary school when he made his famous one-handed catch during his rookie season. Running back Tyrone Tracy Jr . remembers his middle school coach showing his team the highlight. He also remembers seeing and replicating a spin move Beckham made in a game against Washington.

 Wide receiver Malik Nabers wasn't even a football fan growing up. But he credits Beckham with getting him into the team. Nabers was 11 years old when Beckham exploded onto the scene as a rookie. He has since followed in Beckham's footsteps at LSU and the Giants.

 "He kind of was the base person that literally made me start watching football," Nabers said. "The dances, the one-handers. And he was probably the first person I started really watching when I started playing football. He was the main person. So, just for him being here right now, in the same room as me, it's surreal. Sometimes I got to take a moment, but to have him here is actually amazing." 

 The fans seem to be enjoying it as well. When the Giants made their way off the field following a joint practice in Miami several weeks back, fans were chanting "OBJ! OBJ! OBJ!"

 Fans also lined up several hundred deep to pay for a glimpse of OBJ at the  Brian Burns  Celebrity Softball Game in late May that included a signature and picture.

 Superfan Joe Ruback, aka License Plate Guy, arranged for Beckham to attend. Beckham signed and posed for hours until every last fan request was met. He was by far the most popular player in attendance. Beckham then went down onto the field and mingled with his future teammates. He agreed to sign with the team the next day. 

 This is part of the package for a player who has 16.5 million Instagram followers. It doesn't matter if he's now the fourth or fifth receiver on the depth chart.

 Beckham even has a special place in the heart of the team's ownership group. Owner John Mara said years ago his grandchildren cried when Beckham was traded to the Browns. It was totally different for them when Beckham made the team last week.

 "Mr. Mara, he says his grandsons were super happy because they've been kind of asking him every day, 'Is Odell going to make it? Is Odell going to make it?'" coach John Harbaugh said. "I think Mr. Mara's happy. He has a great relationship with Odell, and as you said, the people who were here know the whole history. For us, it's new, we don't know the Giants history as much. But it seems to me like the Maras and the people that were here before are excited ... for Odell."

 Despite his name and popularity, Beckham went out of his way this summer to blend in seamlessly. He wanted to concentrate on football and lay low until he made the team. He limited the number of interviews he gave -- and tabled the dancing and excessive celebrations he was once known for. 

 Staying on the field has been a challenge for Beckham. He's torn his ACL twice and broke his leg earlier in his career. Beckham didn't play in 2022 and 2025, and appeared in just 23 games over the past four seasons.

 Beckham has talked over the years about investing massive amounts of money into his body.

 He trained rigorously in Arizona this offseason to get in the best possible playing shape for this season. It paid dividends this summer, when he remained healthy and regularly hit over 20 miles per hours. He told ESPN that he'll get to 21 miles per hour eventually.

 Beckham participated in every practice this summer. And with that, each day he was dissected as if he were the No. 1 receiver. He admitted there was an unfamiliar pressure. It was evident when he let out a scream after catching a touchdown pass from Jameis Winston late in training camp.

 "No matter what, people are going to talk about me regardless, good, bad, whatever it is," Beckham said. "It just kind of comes with the nature of truly the hard work that I put in to be able to have that opportunity for someone to speak about me, even on a bad day, slow news days. Sometimes people are going to use my name to boost their own whatever it is. So, it is what it is. It comes with the territory. My focus will always be just kind of block that out and come here, produce, and be the best me I can be."

 

 All the attention creates outsized expectations. Some seem to think prime Beckham is going to show up on the field next Sunday night for the Giants' season opener against the Dallas Cowboys  -- the same Cowboys team that Beckham made his famous one-handed catch against.

 It wouldn't surprise the believers if he recreated the moment. Or created a comparable highlight.

 "I think he was such an exciting player throughout his career that I feel like it's almost like Steph Curry. Every time you shoot, he thinks he's going to make," Slayton said. "Every time he sticks one hand out, you expect it to just stick to him. Even though it's not reality, whatever. But he has that type of shock and awe, I guess a wow factor, so to speak. But I think he brings a lot of experience. He still has juice, too. I think he's shown that.…

title: Inside Commanders DC Daronte Jones' unusual coaching journey
summary: From living in his car to various college offices, Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones has paid his dues.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- The gale-force Chicago wind shook Daronte Jones' car and rattled his nerves. It did not blow the future  Washington Commanders  defensive coordinator off his path, but it made him question his life choices.

 It was March 2002, nearly three weeks after Jones landed a job at Division III North Park University on the city's northwest side, and he was sleeping in a red 1988 Honda Prelude.

 He endured a night that ended up steeling his resolve as winds reached 50 mph. At around 11 p.m., he called his aunt Lisa Simmons in Maryland.

 "She picked up thinking it was an emergency, which it really wasn't, but it could have been, mentally," Jones said. "The car was rocking side to side.

 "I remember calling home and naturally the family was like, 'Just come home. What are we doing?' That was a moment where you really had to think about how much you're willing to sacrifice, and is it worth it?"

 Jones didn't go home.

 That was the first decision in a long list of sacrifices the first-time NFL defensive coordinator had to make early in his coaching career. He lived out of his car for two months in Chicago. Then, in 2010, while a grad assistant at UCLA, he slept in the cornerbacks' meeting room for most of his year with the Bruins. Two years after that, as a University of Hawaii assistant, he slept in his office for a year before moving into an alumnus' pool house.

 Along his journey -- often with his pet python, Goldie Gambino, living in his book bag -- he also coached high school for two years and nearly left the profession twice -- attending law school at one point, and applying to the U.S. Capitol Police at another in hopes of becoming a Federal Air Marshal. However, like on that frigid night in the Windy City, he always resolved to stick it out.

 "It was like, 'Is it ever going to end?'" Jones told ESPN. "I was like, 'Maybe it's not for me.'"

 The big breaks finally came, which have led Jones, who is a native of Anne Arundel County in Maryland, to Washington, where he has been entrusted with improving a defense that was arguably the worst in the NFL last season. His background could be a good match for the task ahead.

 A turbulent start to his career helped him develop a deep appreciation for future opportunities -- and for finally reaching this point in his career. It taught him patience; it taught him humility.

 "It's very easy to see when someone has been through it to get to where they're at," safety Jeremy Reaves said. "He went the route not a lot of people go for. How he is on the field is what you'd expect: the sense of urgency. He understands what an opportunity means. He understands opportunities are few and far between, so when you get one, you have to take advantage."

 

 

 BEFORE ARRIVING IN  Washington, Jones had held 14 different jobs during his coaching career, from Division II to Division I-AA, high school, the Canadian Football League to multiple Division I stops and stints with three NFL teams.

 But one of the most formative roles isn't included on his résumé: North Park University.

 Jones spent six months at the tiny school in 2002, but left before coaching a game.

 When he arrived at North Park as a defensive assistant, Jones, fresh off a graduate assistant role at Lenoir-Rhyne University in Hickory, North Carolina, was told he could sleep on a couch in an apartment with other coaches. Jones didn't trust the couch, which, he said, had looked like it had been pulled off the street -- so he slept in his Prelude.

 He spent his first two months at the school sleeping in the car. He kept a suitcase in his locker but other clothes in the Honda -- along with his nearly 3-foot pet Albino Burmese python. Jones said he would park his car near the facility in a different spot each night. On cold nights, he said he'd crack the windows for airflow, turn on the heat and try to stay warm.

 Simmons often lent him money when she could. But she said Jones told her, "'I'll just work it out; I'll stay in the car.' He said, 'All I need you to do is call me and wake me up.' So I would get up early and call him, 'Daronte, it's time to get up.' We really wanted things to work out for him, and he was willing to make the sacrifice. We would support him the best we could."

 Simmons never wavered. Every morning at 4 a.m., Jones would receive a call from his aunt, then head to the facility to shower before others arrived.

 Throughout this time, Jones said he had been telling the other coaches on staff he was living in a hotel. When some found out he wasn't, they offered him the pantry in their apartment, which was on the porch and attached to the kitchen with screens that needed fixing. Jones said the room was full of boxes and was so narrow, his double mattress couldn't lie flat -- it was curled on the outside because it wouldn't fit.

 His grandfather told him how to fix and seal the screens, and Jones bought a space heater to keep him and Goldie Gambino comfortable. "I'd sleep in jeans, sweats, a hoodie, leather jacket to stay warm," Jones said. "But it was better than the car."

 Four months later, he accepted a restricted earnings job at Nicholls State. Though the opportunity at North Park might have seemed to be a waste, having never coached a game for the Vikings, the sacrifices Jones made in Chicago became a key theme throughout the rest of his journey.

 

 

 JONES NEARLY DROPPED out of coaching -- twice.

 The first time occurred in 2004 when he was 25 and coaching defense at Jeanerette High School in New Iberia, Louisiana. It was his first year at Jeanerette but second year coaching high school in Louisiana. Jones had given himself a deadline: become a college Division 1 position coach by age 26 or quit.

 He took the LSAT with plans to attend Southern University's law school with an Omega Psi Phi fraternity brother. Then, Mike Lynn, who was Jones' former position coach at Morgan State, where he played offensive line, became the head coach at Bowie State. Their connection led to a job offer. But Jones said he wasn't sure that he wanted to accept. He could continue teaching in high school, then attend law school classes at night.

 Zeb Simon, Jones' boss at Jeanerette, told him it was a no-brainer and issued him an ultimatum.

 "I'm going to give you a choice," Simon said. "Either you go or I'm going to fire you.'"

 Jones went.

 "It took me about a couple weeks to make that decision," he said.

 

 Five seasons into his stint with the Bulldogs as assistant head coach and defensive coordinator -- the last of which saw his defense ranked No. 1 in Division II -- Jones reached another crossroads. The move to Division I wasn't happening. So, after the 2009 season, he applied for a job with the U.S. Capitol Police, hoping to become a Federal Air Marshal. He had received an offer, and they were in the process of doing a background check when UCLA called.

 "Maybe it's time for me to look at something else because now I'm in my 30s, and I was like: 'I've got to do something,'" Jones said he was thinking at the time.

 The Bruins offered him a graduate assistant's job. It meant going from a salary of $64,000 a year to $1,000 per month while living in the Los Angeles area. He first consulted Damon Wilson, his boss in 2009 at Bowie State, about the UCLA opportunity. But it was longtime advisor Lional Vital, who spent part of four seasons in the NFL and also served as a scout and executive for 30 years, who convinced him.

 "You've already been homeless," Vital told him.

 Unable to afford the cost of living in Southern California, Jones made his "home" in the UCLA cornerbacks' meeting room, where he spent most of the year sleeping on an air mattress alongside another graduate assistant, Chris Polizzi -- now Iowa's special teams coordinator -- who slept on a futon. The arrangement disappointed Wilson.
